entries.section: (1) The places where the commandments were given

paragraphs.text: Beyond the Jordan: the eastern bank of the Jordan River.
The wilderness: the barren desert.

The plain (Arabah): the valley (plain) extending from the southern end of the Dead Sea to the Gulf of Aqaba. Suph: what is meant here is the Gulf of Aqaba; the name Sea of Suph is applied to the whole Red Sea, or to the gulf as part of the sea.

Paran: the name of the desert extending through the eastern region of the Sinai Peninsula, parallel to the line running from El-Arish to Eilat (anciently Ezion-geber). Tophel: a place about 20 km south-east of the Dead Sea; it may be the present village of Tafileh, which has 600 inhabitants.
Laban: or Libnah, which lies a few kilometres north-east of Hazeroth.
Hazeroth: about 40 km north-east of Mount Horeb; it is where Miriam, the sister of Moses, became leprous (Num 12) (maps 1, 12).

Dizahab: on the line of march from Sinai to Kadesh-barnea, among the mountains, between the wilderness of Paran to the west and the Gulf of Aqaba to the east. Its meaning is "the place where there is much gold."
These are the commandments of Moses to his people before his departure from this world, and they are for the people of God in every generation.

Moses specified the place where he met with the people and spoke to them in three sermons (and to simplify matters for the reader we say that this place is east of the Jordan River). Here begins the first of these sermons, which is recorded in (ch. 1-5). He probably spoke to the elders of Israel and not to the whole people, whose number exceeded 2 million persons, and the seventy elders conveyed his words to all the people.

We shall notice in this sermon, although it is the farewell address of Moses, who had reached the age of 120 years and whose life was drawing to its end, that he did not speak of his own achievements and his labor with his people, but spoke of God's love and care for them, so that the people would remember this and not be distracted from God by the good things of the Promised Land into which they were about to enter. Moses also did not speak of the wars they would fight to possess the Promised Land, but spoke of God's care for them; for what matters is their relationship with God, and by His power victory in all wars will be easy for them.

entries.section: (1) The places where the commandments were given

paragraphs.text: Eleven days: a traveler on foot walks about 8 hours a day, covering 20 miles in them, or 15 miles if they are a caravan. The distance between Horeb and Kadesh-barnea is 165 miles, so it takes 11 days.
Horeb: the region around Mount Sinai, on which Moses received the Ten Commandments.
Mount Seir: south of the Dead Sea.
Kadesh-barnea: in the middle of the line extending from El-Arish to the head of the Gulf of Aqaba.

The journey between Horeb and Kadesh-barnea takes 11 days, but the journey of the children of Israel in Sinai took 40 years. This was because of the hardness of their hearts and their refusal to obey God by entering the Promised Land and rooting out the wicked, so God made them wander in the wilderness until the stubborn generation died and their sons entered the Promised Land.

It is to be noted that the Book of Deuteronomy consists of teachings from Moses to the new people after the death of all the fathers, except Joshua the son of Nun and Caleb the son of Jephunneh. In this it differs from the books of Exodus, Leviticus and Numbers, in which we hear of God's conversations with Moses. Here he strengthens the people in faith in God and in holding fast to His commandments and laws, so that they would not be alarmed by the might of the enemies in the land of Canaan, nor forget His laws amid the pagan worship prevalent in Canaan.

Be obedient to God's commandments however difficult they may seem, for they are the shortest way to enter the Kingdom, and be confident that God will support you and deliver you from every evil if you obey His commandments.

entries.section: (2) Remembering the defeat of Sihon and Og

paragraphs.text: The addresses of Moses to his people took place at the end of the fortieth year after the children of Israel left Egypt. He repeated to them the rulings of the divine Law which he had transmitted to them, and followed them with his counsel that they should not turn aside from it and his warning to them of what would befall them if they transgressed it. The timing of these addresses was a short time before his repose and the handing over of leadership to Joshua.

Moses began his address on the first day of the eleventh month of the fortieth year, and the people crossed the Jordan River and entered the Promised Land on the tenth day of the first month of the forty-first year (Josh 4:19). The whole period is therefore sixty-nine days. Moses spent about thirty days in the addresses recorded in the Book of Deuteronomy, and they mourned for him thirty days (ch. 34:8), and in the few remaining days the Law was written and handed over to the Levites.

entries.section: (2) Remembering the defeat of Sihon and Og

paragraphs.text: The Amorites: a Semitic people of Canaanite origin. In the time of Moses they lived in the south of Palestine, and at some period of their history they also ruled the region east of the Jordan, from the Arnon River in the south to Mount Hermon in the north.
Heshbon: the city of Sihon king of the Amorites in the time of Moses. In its place today is a ruined city known as "Hesban," between the Arnon River and the Jabbok River.

Bashan: a province in the land of Canaan lying east of the Jordan between Mount Hermon and Mount Gilead, bounded on the north by Damascus, on the east by the Syrian desert, on the south by the land of Gilead and on the west by the Jordan River, and crossed in the east by the Druze Mountain (map 5). Astaroth: a town in Bashan that was the capital of Og king of Bashan; it is thought to be the present Tell Ashtara, 35 km east of the Sea of Galilee.
Edrei: the capital of Bashan, whose present name is "Daraa"; it lies about 47 km east of the southern end of the Sea of Galilee, on the border between Jordan and Syria.

Beyond the Jordan: the eastern bank of the Jordan (maps 4, 13). The people, under the leadership of Moses, reached this spot, which lies on the eastern bank of the Jordan in the land of Moab, after two wars in which Israel defeated both Sihon king of the Amorites and Og king of Bashan. Sihon controlled the southern part east of the Jordan River while Og ruled its northern part. The news of this victory is given in the Book of Numbers (ch. 21) (map 5).

entries.section: (2) Remembering the defeat of Sihon and Og

paragraphs.text: The land of Moab: the eastern part of the Dead Sea region, which is today part of the Kingdom of Jordan. Moses was not content to repeat the Law, but also explained and interpreted it for the new generation, which was about to enter the land of Canaan after the previous generation had perished entirely in the wilderness.
It is good to remember God's former works with you, so that you may be reassured, give thanks and take courage in your striving, relying on His power.

entries.section: (3) God's call to enter the land of Canaan

paragraphs.text: The children of Israel reached Mount Horeb on the first day of the third month in the first year of their departure from Egypt, and they remained there about a year, during which they received the commandments and the Law and made the Tabernacle of Meeting as God had commanded them. But afterwards they refused to enter the Promised Land, so He made them wander in the wilderness of Sinai for 40 years.

entries.section: (3) God's call to enter the land of Canaan

paragraphs.text: The mount of the Amorites: it is in the south of Palestine, and the Amorites had five kings in it (Josh 10:5). The Arabah: the great rift in which the Jordan River flows.

The mountains, the plain and the south: the plain is the low-lying lands adjoining the Mediterranean Sea and extending from the north of Palestine to its south; the mountains are the central highlands; and the south is the Negev region extending from the south of Palestine to the border of Egypt.
The seaside: the coastal regions on the Mediterranean Sea.

The land of Canaan: what is meant by it is all the land of Palestine and its surroundings, inhabited by the Canaanite peoples. Lebanon to the great river, the river Euphrates: what is meant is present-day Lebanon, which extends along the Mediterranean coast, and then the lands extending east of it as far as the Euphrates River.

The Lord asked them to journey and enter the mount of the Amorites in the south of Palestine and head north to the great river, that is, the Euphrates River; this is the land promised to the fathers Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, for the Lord longed to hasten to fulfill His promise to give them possession of the land.

Unbelief in God's promises makes us stray from His commandments, so that we wander in this world and are exposed to being lost in sins and scattered in worldly thoughts that take us away from the way of life which God has drawn for us, as He said, "I am the way, the truth, and the life," and thus we walk in labyrinths that take us away from the Kingdom which the Lord promised to those who obey His commandments.

entries.section: (4) The appointment of elders to help Moses

paragraphs.text: Before continuing the events of the main story, whose beginning is mentioned in (vv. 6-8) and which tells what happened when the Lord asked them to enter the Promised Land and possess it, Moses turns to another event that also took place at Horeb, the appointment of a number of judges to decide the cases of the people (Ex 18:13-27); for it was very difficult for Moses alone to judge and resolve the problems of 2 million souls.

entries.section: (4) The appointment of elders to help Moses

paragraphs.text: As He has spoken to you: He promised your fathers.

The number of the people increased greatly, as God had promised Abraham, and consequently the problems that inevitably arise among individuals and groups so numerous also increased; this is natural with the growth in numbers. Moses blesses them and asks God to increase their numbers more and more.

entries.section: (4) The appointment of elders to help Moses

paragraphs.text: Moses decided to take the counsel of his father-in-law (Jethro) (the story recorded in Ex 18:13-27), so he appointed a number of wise men to help him in deciding disputes, and the people welcomed this.

entries.section: (4) The appointment of elders to help Moses

paragraphs.text: Known men (heads): persons who knew the word of God so as to judge by it among their brethren. They were probably like counselors who judged for all the tribes, that is, for the people in general and not for a particular group, and they were distinguished in understanding and knowledge. Many of them may have been among the foremen who led the people of Israel in Egypt to gather bricks and build the cities which the Egyptians forced them to build (Ex 5:6).
Hear: give attention to hearing the complaints and problems of the people, so that you may judge and resolve them for them.

Moses divided the people into small groups, that is, tens, and appointed a judge over each; then over every few groups he appointed a higher judge, and so on until he appointed a judge ruling over thousands of them. He also appointed general counselors whom he called heads, and gave them much advice for this work of theirs, and commanded them to hold fast to the truth in their judgments, without any ulterior purpose, whether between the Jews and one another or between them and the strangers dwelling among them. It is to be noted that God did not choose them from the rich or those of high position, but chose them for their wisdom, discernment, understanding and care for His word, so that they might teach the people by it.

entries.section: (4) The appointment of elders to help Moses

paragraphs.text: For the judgment is God's: you are judges on God's behalf, to judge by His word, so you must be just as He is.
These instructions were not to show partiality in judgment and not to fear any man in their judging, however high his standing, and to bring to him every matter too hard for them to judge.

Let us not despise the counsels offered to us by others, even if they are of lower standing than we are, just as Moses the leader accepted the counsel of his pagan father-in-law; nor let us scorn them, but accept what is good in them in a spirit of humility, so that we benefit from the counsel of others.

entries.section: (5) Sending spies to explore the land

paragraphs.text: The great and terrible wilderness: the northern regions of the wilderness of Sinai, which are rugged and wide, and passing through them is dangerous because they are barren and have wild beasts, in addition to the wicked peoples living in and around it; but God by His care preserved them in it.

The mount of the Amorites: one of the most important landmarks of the way in this wilderness, which we have mentioned in (v. 7) (map 1). Moses resumes the main story in this chapter, so the present verses can be read directly after (vv. 6-8) in order to follow the continuity of the story.
The people departed from Horeb as the Lord commanded and came to Kadesh-barnea (maps 1, 12).

entries.section: (5) Sending spies to explore the land

paragraphs.text: Here Moses made them understand that by this they had reached the mount of the Amorites, which the Lord had promised them would be the first stage of the way to their possessing the land, and therefore it is the gateway leading to the rest of the promised land.

entries.section: (5) Sending spies to explore the land

paragraphs.text: Moses reassures them that there is no need for fear or dread in facing the inhabitants of the land, because it is the Lord who commanded them to go up and possess the land.

entries.section: (5) Sending spies to explore the land

paragraphs.text: The people did not carry out God's command immediately to go up and possess the land, but decided to send out a reconnaissance party to spy out the land before entering it as warriors. This may have been sound military thinking, practiced even in our present world, but the motive for sending the spies was their fear of the unknown in the new land, because of the weakness of their faith in God and their disobedience to Him. When they asked Moses to send spies, he spoke to God, and God agreed, not because this was the right course of action but because of His longsuffering toward the people (Num 13:1, 2). Sadly, when the spies returned, ten of them proclaimed the strength of the enemies and the impossibility of overcoming them, so the people were afraid and followed them, and rejected the encouragement of Joshua the son of Nun and Caleb the son of Jephunneh, the two spies who showed the blessing of God and His good things in the land and His power able to support the people. When the people murmured against God, He was angry with them and did not bring them into the Promised Land, but made them wander in the wilderness until all the murmurers died, and only their sons entered the Promised Land.

entries.section: (5) Sending spies to explore the land

paragraphs.text: Therefore Moses agreed with them in this and sent the party, choosing one man from each tribe.

entries.section: (5) Sending spies to explore the land

paragraphs.text: The valley of Eshcol: a valley near Hebron to the north, still famous today for its vineyards; it is the valley of Hebron or the valley of Mamre (map 2).

They went up to the mount of the Amorites and came to the valley of Eshcol. The Book of Numbers gave the details of the places through which the spies passed, and their journey took forty days (Num 13:21-25).

entries.section: (5) Sending spies to explore the land

paragraphs.text: They took samples of the fruit of the land and its abundant good things, then returned to their tribes saying that the land was good and fruitful.

If you become troubled by anything, do not stir up those around you and do not yield to thoughts of doubt and tension, but turn to God in prayer and ask for the guidance of your father of confession, so that you may calm down and God may guide you to the right solution and you may guide those around you, so that you become a cause of blessing to others and not of disturbance.

entries.section: (6) Their refusal to enter the Promised Land

paragraphs.text: Despite what the spies brought as confirmation of the truth of the Lord's promises that the land was good, "flowing with milk and honey," the weakness of the people's faith made them not trust the Lord's call to them to enter the land; on the contrary, they thought of appointing a leader for themselves other than Moses in order to return to Egypt (Num 14:1-4).

entries.section: (6) Their refusal to enter the Promised Land

paragraphs.text: The sons of Anak: the descendants of Anak, a Canaanite man. They were described as giants because of their tall stature and the might of their strength in wars, and they are proverbial for their multitude and enormous size. They lived in the south of Palestine between Jerusalem and Hebron.

When they heard the spies say that the people of the land were very strong, that the cities were completely fortified against any foreign invasion and that the sons of Anak lived there, they were very afraid.

entries.section: (6) Their refusal to enter the Promised Land

paragraphs.text: Moses reassured them, since he trusted in the Lord, and he had warned them before not to fear or be afraid of the inhabitants of the land.

entries.section: (6) Their refusal to enter the Promised Land

paragraphs.text: Moses reminded them of all the works which the Lord had done with them and which they had witnessed with their own eyes since they were in Egypt, and that it was He who led them in the wilderness by the pillar of cloud and the pillar of fire, and it was He who would bring them into the land of Canaan by His great power.

entries.section: (6) Their refusal to enter the Promised Land

paragraphs.text: Moses also reminded them of God's care for them in the wilderness of Sinai, and how He fed them with manna and gave them drink from the rock and preserved their clothes and their sandals, and they passed safely on the way until He brought them to the threshold of the Promised Land. He likened God's care for them to a man who carries his child in his arms and looks after all his needs, so that he lacks nothing.

entries.section: (6) Their refusal to enter the Promised Land

paragraphs.text: Moses rebuked them for their lack of faith in God's power which had led them in the wilderness of Sinai by the pillar of cloud by day and the pillar of fire by night, and how He chose for them suitable places to settle. Now He has prepared for them the land of Canaan, filled with good things, and by His power He is able to bring them into it; so why are they afraid?!

It may appear to us during our journey in life that the way of the Kingdom is a hard way, for it is a way of continual warfare against the enemy of good, which requires of us spiritual striving and constant vigilance, so we fear and shrink from walking in this hard way and forget that God is our defender and that the wars are the Lord's wars. Let us have complete confidence in God's victory over the world, as the Lord Christ assured us, saying, "Be of good cheer; I have overcome the world."

entries.section: (7) God's punishment of them for refusing to enter the Promised Land

paragraphs.text: The people's conduct in this situation brought upon them the wrath of the Lord, so He inflicted the punishment fitting for this disobedience.

entries.section: (7) God's punishment of them for refusing to enter the Promised Land

paragraphs.text: When God saw the people's murmuring and their attempt to return to Egypt, He declared that all of them were deprived of entering the Promised Land, except the two who believed in Him and encouraged the people. One of them is mentioned here, Caleb the son of Jephunneh, who would possess the land on which he had trodden, that is, he would take his portion of the land of Canaan. In this verse He did not mention "Joshua," his companion, but will mention him in (v. 38), because he would not only enter the Promised Land but would lead the whole people as successor to Moses.

entries.section: (7) God's punishment of them for refusing to enter the Promised Land

paragraphs.text: For your sakes: because of your frequent murmuring, I was driven to strike the rock twice and sinned against God.

In humility, Moses shows his weakness in striking the rock twice at Meribah (Num 20:10-12), contrary to God's command; for he was strained by the repeated murmurings of the children of Israel and struck the rock twice instead of once. Therefore God deprived him of entering the Promised Land because of the weakness of his faith. But this did not diminish the greatness of Moses, whom the Church considers the chief of the prophets and who is the greatest figure in the eyes of the Jews. All this confirms the gravity of the murmuring into which the children of Israel fell and of their disobedience to God.

entries.section: (7) God's punishment of them for refusing to enter the Promised Land

paragraphs.text: Who stands before you: your disciple who assists you.

Encourage him: Moses laid his hands on Joshua, encouraged him and gave him counsels, and did all this before the people as a declaration that he was his successor, so that they would respect him and submit to him (Num 27:20, 22, 23; Deut 31:7, 8). God commanded Moses to strengthen Joshua and declare before the people that he was his successor, to lead the children of Israel after him and bring them into the Promised Land.

entries.section: (7) God's punishment of them for refusing to enter the Promised Land

paragraphs.text: God will fulfill His promise in the next generation, those who were children at that time, that is, less than twenty years old, whom the fathers feared would fall into captivity or be killed in the battles with the sons of Anak. The Lord promises that these sons will inherit the Promised Land because they are innocent of the disobedience of their fathers, for their young age at that time did not allow them to know good and evil.

entries.section: (7) God's punishment of them for refusing to enter the Promised Land

paragraphs.text: Since God was angry with the people, He kept them away from the Promised Land and turned them into the wilderness of Sinai toward the Red Sea, to wander in this wilderness for about 40 years, during which all the adults who murmured would die; then He would bring their sons back to the threshold of the Promised Land, where Moses is now speaking to them before his death and just before their entering the Promised Land.

Do not make light of God's longsuffering by murmuring against your life and refusing to carry out His commandments, for He is just and able to deprive you of many blessings which you enjoy now. If you fall into murmuring, return quickly to Him in repentance and thank Him for His gifts, because He is a tender Father who wants to forgive you all your sins.

entries.section: (8) The defeat of Israel before the peoples of the land

paragraphs.text: The children of Israel realized their error toward God when He declared His wrath against them by depriving them of entering the Promised Land, but they did not repent; rather, they rushed to enter the Promised Land without praying and seeking God's help. They felt their strength after arming themselves, putting on belts and weapons of war, and made light of going up the mountain and attacking the enemies, trusting in their own strength and not in God.

entries.section: (8) The defeat of Israel before the peoples of the land

paragraphs.text: When God saw their rushing to fight the enemies relying on their own strength, He had compassion on them in His fatherhood and warned them against entering the Promised Land, for this was not obedience to His commands but rashness and pride on their part. He warned them that He would not be with them and therefore they would be defeated before the enemies.

entries.section: (8) The defeat of Israel before the peoples of the land

paragraphs.text: You were presumptuous: you were proud and insolent.

God reminded them that they had not obeyed Him, but in pride trusted in their own strength and rushed toward the mountains in the south of Palestine to go up them, fight the enemies and possess their land.
(map 13)

entries.section: (8) The defeat of Israel before the peoples of the land

paragraphs.text: Hormah: on the border of Edom near Ziklag.

The land of Seir: a land that the Horites inhabited (Gen 14:6), then Esau and his descendants took possession of it (Gen 32:3); it was also called Mount Seir, and the land of Seir lies south of the Dead Sea (map 13). God reminded them that when they disobeyed Him and attacked the Amorites, the Amorites came out against them and drove them from their land, as bees drive away anyone who attacks their hives, and kept pursuing them as far as Hormah, a town on the border of the land of Edom in the south of Palestine. When the children of Israel returned in great sorrow after many of them had been killed, God did not listen to their cry because they had not repented.

entries.section: (8) The defeat of Israel before the peoples of the land

paragraphs.text: The children of Israel stayed in Kadesh with hearts full of grief over their defeat before the enemies, for many days, which some think were forty days, like the period they spent in Kadesh waiting for the spies to return from their mission of spying out the Promised Land. After that they journeyed in the wilderness for about 38 years in wandering until all the murmuring people died, and then they returned again to Kadesh so that the sons might enter the Promised Land.

The enemy of good often makes us imagine that our earthly wisdom is better than divine counsel, so we make decisions and walk in ways that do not agree with what God has drawn for us, and after entering into temptation the error of our choices and the troubles they have caused us become clear to us. Let us always set God's will before our eyes and leave the leadership to Him to direct our life according to His good will.
The march of victory over Sihon king of the Amorites

God led His people by the pillar of cloud and the pillar of fire, so they headed south toward the Red Sea (the Gulf of Aqaba) and went around the Seir mountain range, which lies in the land of Edom in the south of Palestine (maps 1, 13), and they began their journey in the wilderness of Sinai, to wander in it about 38 years, for the following reasons:
1- The death of all the men from twenty years old and upward, who were the ones who murmured against God.
2- The sons' experience of God's care, to confirm their faith in Him.
3- The sons' estrangement from Egypt and its pagan worship, and the offering of worship to the one God in the Tabernacle of Meeting.
4- Victory over some peoples such as Amalek, Sihon king of the Amorites and Og king of Bashan, to confirm their faith and prepare them to enter the Promised Land and gain victory over its peoples.

In the thirty-ninth year after their departure from Egypt, and after the death of the whole former generation, which had feared to carry out the Lord's command to enter the Promised Land, the Lord asked them to end their circling in the wilderness of Sinai and head north again toward the Promised Land, to begin carrying out the plan He had drawn for them to enter the land.

Our sojourn in the world is a temporary period, after which we return to heaven; therefore we must prepare throughout our life for our eternal life, and not indulge in the passing desires of the world nor be occupied with its labyrinths that never end, but always remember our only goal, which is to be with God on earth in preparation for being with Him forever in heaven.

In their course northward the people had to pass within the borders of the land of Esau, which is the region of Seir. The Edomites' fear of the congregation of Israel was due to their great number and to the awe God had cast upon His people which frightens enemies, and this reminds us of what is written in (Gen 35:5) concerning the awe of Jacob and his sons during their journeys. But God sternly warns them against attacking the Edomites, because He will not allow them to take the lands of the sons of Esau, since He had already given those lands to him as an inheritance (Josh 24:4). Here God explains to His children the reason for the prohibition; He is not content to issue commands to His beloved, but shares with them the knowledge of the reasons, and also teaches them:
1- Not to be proud because the Edomites fear them and so rush to fight them, for this awe is a grace from God and not from themselves.

2- To value the bond of brotherhood, because Esau is the brother of Jacob and so their descendants are brothers; although the sons of Esau had gone on to worship idols, the sons of Jacob should keep their love for them.

The Lord has blessed you in all the works of your hand: whether the raising of sheep or the wealth they took from the Egyptians (Ex 12:35, 36) and what they gained as spoil from Amalek after their victory over them (Ex 17:13). The Lord stressed that their dealing with the descendants of Esau should be with complete integrity and regard for their rights; if they bought anything from them, they should give them their due in the price and take nothing by force, knowing that in reality they had no need of this, for the Lord had provided them everything they needed during their journey in the wilderness, so the people felt no want or need of anything throughout the years of wandering. He gave them manna from heaven and water from the rock, yet did not prevent them from eating anything else they found in the wilderness; so if they wished to eat anything of the Edomites' produce, they were to buy it from them.
Elath: the present Eilat, at the northern end of the Gulf of Aqaba.

Ezion-geber: west of the port of Eilat, at present "Tell el-Kheleifeh" (map 1). The children of Israel tried to pass through the land of the Edomites, but they refused, so Israel did not fight them as God commanded, but went around their country from the plain extending west of the Dead Sea until they reached the north of the Gulf of Aqaba, then headed north to the east of the Dead Sea, to the land of Moab (Num 20:14-21).
May you value family relationships and kinship, and show love to everyone even if they have wronged you, for you love them for the sake of God, who gives you many blessings in your life.
Ar: one of the largest cities of Moab; it is also called Aroer and lies near its northern border, and was later called "Rabbath-moab"; it is now in ruins.

The Lord warned the children of Israel, on their way to the wilderness of Moab, not to stir up war against the Moabites, just as He had warned them before concerning the Edomites, and He also showed them the reason, which is that He had already given them their land as an inheritance, because Moab was the son of Lot by his elder daughter, and Lot was the righteous man whom God wished to honor in his descendants because he followed the way of the Lord and tormented his soul day and night by what he saw around him of the conduct of the wicked. In addition there was the kinship that links Lot to Abraham, their forefather, for he was his brother's son.
The Emims: they lived in the same region which the Moabites inhabited after them. They were a great and strong people and are also called Rephaims.
The Anakims: they are the sons of Anak who were described in the first chapter. The Anakims are one of the branches of the Rephaims.

He mentions the inhabitants of the land, who were the Emims, and likens them in their multitude and strength to the Anakims, and mentions that they are also called Rephaims because the Anakims are of the descendants of the Rephaims. God's mention of these ancient peoples who inhabited the land is not merely a historical account of the inhabitants of the land, but is to confirm and strengthen the faith of His people: just as these ancient peoples passed away, so God will remove the pagan inhabitants of the land of Canaan and drive them out from before His people.
The Horims: the original inhabitants of Mount Seir; the descendants of Esau destroyed them and dwelt in their place.

Just as the Book of Deuteronomy told us in the preceding verses the original inhabitants of the land of the Moabites, it returns here and also tells us the original inhabitants of the land of the Edomites, who were the Horims. But when God decided to give that land to the Edomites to dwell in, He allowed the sons of Esau, according to His eternal plan, to overcome them and dwell in their place, and so too He will give the land of Canaan to the children of Israel and drive out of it the pagans who inhabit the land.
Be faithful over all God's gifts to you so that He may bless you, but if you neglect them, God will take them from you and give them to one who deserves them.

entries.section: (4) The perishing of the generation that came out of Egypt

paragraphs.text: The brook Zered: the Zered is a small river that rises from Mount Abarim east of the Dead Sea and flows into it; it marks the border between Edom and Moab and is now called "Wadi el-Hasa" (map 1).

The Lord guided the people at every step of their way toward the Promised Land, so when they reached that point after safely passing through the lands of the Edomites and the Moabites, the Lord asked them to rise up and cross the brook Zered.

entries.section: (4) The perishing of the generation that came out of Egypt

paragraphs.text: The period that had passed since they left "Kadesh" was thirty-eight years, during which all the men of the generation that disobeyed the Lord by refusing to enter the land died.

Then they returned to Kadesh-barnea and crossed the Zered River; for their first coming to Kadesh-barnea was in the second year after their departure from Egypt, and they wandered in the wilderness of Sinai 38 years, then returned to Kadesh-barnea in the fortieth year after their departure from Egypt, where Aaron died in the fifth month, and then they crossed the Zered River (Num 33:38).

entries.section: (4) The perishing of the generation that came out of Egypt

paragraphs.text: The camp: the place where the tents of the children of Israel are pitched.

The death of the men from twenty years old and upward was not due to old age alone, but the wrath of God came upon them and destroyed many of them, such as the death of the ten spies who spread murmuring among the people (Num 14:36, 37), and such as the death of Korah, Dathan, Abiram and the two hundred and fifty with them, whom the earth swallowed (Num 16); and a great number of them also died by the plague (Num 25:9).

The disobedience of the children of Israel to God's word deprived them of entering the Promised Land; so do not refuse to obey God's commandments because your mind rejects them or they conflict with your desires, lest you deprive yourself of happiness and of obtaining the Kingdom of Heaven.

entries.section: (5) Not attacking the children of Ammon

paragraphs.text: When the generation that disobeyed the Lord had perished, the people were about to pass by the border of the land of Moab, passing through the city of "Ar," which is near the northern border of the land of Moab. The country of the children of Ammon lies north-west of the land of Moab (map 14).

Sea of Tiberias Yarmuk The Great Sea Jordan River Gilead Canaan Jabbok ● Heshbon Jahaz● ● Kedemoth A map showing the locations Aroer● Arnon ● taken by Sihon king of Heshbon from Ar Wadi Zered map (14)

entries.section: (5) Not attacking the children of Ammon

paragraphs.text: Here too He warns them against showing enmity to the Ammonites or attacking them, because they are their kin and God gave them this land and will not allow the children of Israel to take it from them, for they are the sons of Lot, the son of their forefather Abraham's brother, by his younger daughter (Gen 19:38).

entries.section: (5) Not attacking the children of Ammon

paragraphs.text: The Zamzummims: another name for the Rephaims; the Moabites call the Rephaims Emims, and the Ammonites call the Rephaims Zamzummims.

In truth the Emims and the Zamzummims are peoples branching from the Rephaims. The Zamzummims are also called the Zuzims, whom Chedorlaomer defeated (Gen 14:5). The meaning of the name Zamzummims is the "murmurers." Just as the book gave us the names of the original inhabitants of the land of Moab and the land of Edom, it tells us here the original inhabitants of the land of the children of Ammon. The Rephaims dwelt in it formerly, and it describes them as a strong people and likens them in their multitude and tallness to the Anakims mentioned in (v. 10). But God gave the children of Ammon victory over them and gave them their land.

entries.section: (5) Not attacking the children of Ammon

paragraphs.text: Likewise God drove out the Horims, the original inhabitants of the land, from before the sons of Esau and made them dwell in their place.

God drives out the wicked and settles others in their place. If God blesses you, do not be proud, but thank Him and be humble before Him, for if you do evil the wrath of God will come upon you unless you repent.

entries.section: (5) Not attacking the children of Ammon

paragraphs.text: The Avims: an ancient people who dwelt in the region of Gaza.

To confirm the driving out of the wicked peoples and the settling of others in their place, the book here mentions other invaders, the Caphtorims (the ancestors of the Philistines), who are the descendants of Mizraim the son of Ham the son of Noah (Gen 10:14). They came from the island of Crete (Caphtor) or from the Delta of Egypt, which is called (Kaft-Hor), and defeated the original inhabitants of the region of Gaza, who were the Avims. The Lord does not mention here that it was He who gave the Philistines this land, and consequently we find in (Josh 15:47) that this land was assigned to the tribe of Judah along with the rest of the cities of the south (Judg 18:1). God mentioned in this passage the driving out of peoples and the settling of peoples in their place in order to encourage the children of Israel, before whom He will drive out the wicked pagan peoples living in the land of Canaan.
The Amorites: a people who spoke a Semitic language, and it is mentioned in (Gen 10:16) that their lineage goes back to Canaan.

The valley of Arnon: it lies between the Arnon River, which flows into the middle of the Dead Sea on the east, and the Jabbok River, which rises near the present city of Amman and flows into the middle of the Jordan River on the east. This valley, or group of valleys of the Arnon, belonged to the Amorites before the children of Israel took it; the land of Moab lies south of the Arnon River.

Heshbon: the capital of the Amorites, where their king Sihon lived (Num 21:25, 27) (map 14). The Lord continues His leadership of the march of the children of Israel, who had crossed the lands of Moab, Edom and the children of Ammon without stirring up wars against them. And after encouraging them by mentioning the driving out of the ancient peoples and the dwelling of other peoples in their place, He commands them to advance, crossing the valley of Arnon in the direction of the kingdom of Sihon the Amorite, whose command center was the city of "Heshbon." The Lord declares to them that the stage of their taking possession of the lands begins now, and that they must declare war on Sihon. This is the first time that God asks them to fight the pagan inhabitants of the land to take possession of their land, for He had not previously approved of their attacking these inhabitants when they advanced of their own will without God's permission after the spies spied out the land of Canaan 38 years ago, and they were defeated and a great number of them were killed (Num 14:45). The evils of the Amorites were now complete and the time had come for God's wrath to fall on them, for God had said long ago to Abraham, "for the iniquity of the Amorites is not yet full" (Gen 15:16).

God reassures them that He will cast dread upon the inhabitants and kings of those lands which they will possess, so that they will be troubled and alarmed whenever they hear of the approach of the children of Israel to their country.

Here we see that the children of Israel had to fight and strive to possess the land, for it would not be granted to them without effort on their part; but the Lord would not leave them alone in the field, but would be in their midst, granting them victory.

We too must strive in our spiritual warfare against the enemy of good, for spiritual striving is a road on which everyone who seeks the Kingdom walks. We must always arm ourselves with spiritual vigilance to beware of the snares and works of Satan, but victory will not be ours except by the Lord's support of us in our striving, which frightens our enemies, so that the opponent collapses before us and the presence of the Lord is manifested in the midst of His beloved.
Kedemoth: a city east of the Dead Sea lying in the course of the valley of Arnon; it is now called Qasr el-Zafaran (map 14).
The wilderness of Kedemoth: the desert surrounding the city of Kedemoth.

Words of peace: Moses asked of Sihon the same thing he had asked before of the Edomites, the Moabites and the Ammonites, and assured him that he would not take anything from him by force, but that if he needed anything he would buy it from him with money, that is, he would not take anything from him without paying its price (Num 21:21, 22). The action of Moses here in sending messengers to Heshbon with words of peace may raise the question of the reason, and the answer is that this was done by inspiration from God in order to show the hardness that was in Sihon's heart and his not responding to the call of peace, so that he added evils to his evils and deserved to be crushed by God before the warriors of the children of Israel. What God allowed to happen to Sihon and to other peoples who met the same fate was not because God loved the children of Israel at the expense of those peoples; rather, what befell them was the natural fruit of the evils which those nations had committed.
I will go along by the highway, the highway: that is, I will go in a single line from which I will not turn aside to the right or to the left.
Moses asked to walk in a straight line without deviation, and if he needed anything he would buy it with money.
He reminds him that he had acted in this way before with the Ammonites and the Moabites and had not broken his promise, but Sihon refused, and what was in his heart of evil and hardness appeared.

As the Lord promised Moses, His promise was fulfilled, for He gave the children of Israel victory over Sihon and his army. And He says, "Begin to possess": for this was the first land they would possess in Canaan.

Jahaz: a Moabite city between the Arnon and the Jabbok, about 20 km east of the Dead Sea (map 14). Sihon came out to fight the children of Israel at the city of Jahaz; and Sihon, his sons and all his people were killed in the battle, so they no longer existed.
We utterly destroyed: we killed.
Remaining: fleeing.
The children of Israel took all the cities of his kingdom and destroyed in every city all its inhabitants, men, women and children; no one escaped destruction and nothing escaped devastation.
The spoil of war which the children of Israel took from all the cities of the Amorites was the sheep and all the valuable possessions such as silver and gold.
Aroer: a Moabite city to the north of the Arnon River; it is also called Ar (v. 18). It is now called "Ara'ir."
The city that is in the valley: probably Heshbon, the capital of the Amorites.
Gilead: a mountainous region east of the Jordan River (map 14).
There was not one city too strong for us: we took possession of all the land of the Amorites.

The cities in the mountains: the mountainous region at the sources of the Jabbok River, which the Ammonites inhabited. The region which the children of Israel occupied was defined, from Aroer to Gilead. Moses affirms here that he did not touch the region of the children of Ammon adjoining those regions, in the valley of the Jabbok and the cities in the mountains and all the regions belonging to the peoples whom the Lord commanded them not to attack.
The victory over the king of Bashan and the division of the land east of the Jordan

Bashan: a province bounded on the north by Damascus, on the east by Syria, on the south by the land of Gilead, and on the west by the Jordan River; its land was very fertile and its good things many (Num 21:33-35) (map 15). Edrei: the capital of Bashan, lying south-east of the Sea of Galilee.

The children of Israel continued their advance northward to the kingdom of Og king of Bashan, after their victory over Sihon and their taking all his land, as stated in the previous chapter; so the two armies, the army of Israel and the army of Og, met at the city of Edrei.

Strangely, Og did not learn from what happened to Sihon king of the Amorites, but came out to fight the children of Israel instead of allowing them to pass; and this was by God's permission, so that they might defeat him and possess his land.

Og was one of the giants (v. 11), for the king's bedstead was four and a half meters long and two meters wide, so God reassured them as they went to fight him and his army, for he possessed sixty fenced cities in addition to many villages. Here appears the care of God, who reassures His children before tribulations and hard situations.
Remaining: fleeing.
Indeed God fulfilled His promise, and the children of Israel won a complete victory over Og and all who were with him, so that none of them was left alive.

Og rushed to fight the children of Israel relying on his strength and did not take warning from the defeat of Sihon. So be deliberate and examine your affairs so that you do not rush into evil, and learn from the falls of others, and do not be proud whatever your abilities, lest you meet with many troubles and God forsakes you because of your pride and rashness.
The region of Argob: a region in Bashan within the kingdom of Og, which included a large number of fortified cities.
The children of Israel took all the cities and villages of Og, and Moses tells us their count as 60 cities making up the whole region of Bashan, which is the kingdom of Og.
Bars: rods and crossbars for fastening doors securely.

Moses makes clear the greatness of the sixty cities of Og, for they had high walls and huge, firmly fastened gates, in addition to a large number of unwalled villages, all this to show the greatness of the divine victory over Og by means of the people of God, who were weak but strong in their God.

The children of Israel destroyed all the cities and villages of Bashan, and this was by God's command to wipe out the evil and the worship of idols that had pervaded their hearts (ch. 2:34); but they kept the wealth of the cities, including the livestock, and took it all for themselves as spoil of war, for God permitted them this, whereas at other times He commanded them not to take any spoil, in rejection of everything connected with evil, as happened at Jericho (Josh 6:18-21).

Mount Hermon: a mountain extending along the north-eastern boundary of the places which the children of Israel took. It forms the northern end of the Lebanon mountain range, the Jordan River rises from it, and it is said to be the Mount of Transfiguration (map 15). The valley of Arnon: it lies between the Arnon and Jabbok rivers (ch. 2:24) (map 15).

A map showing the places taken from Og Lk Asha map (15) Moses mentions here the land which the children of Israel took from the two kings of the Amorites, Sihon and Og, which is the land lying east of the Jordan River from the valley of the Arnon River in the south to Mount Hermon in the north.
The Sidonians: the inhabitants of Sidon, a Phoenician coastal city between the mountains of Lebanon and the Mediterranean Sea, 30 km north of Tyre.
He mentions other names for Hermon: the people of Sidon call it "Sirion" and the Amorites call it "Shenir."

Salchah: a city marking the eastern boundary of Bashan, which was under the rule of Og king of Bashan; the present Salkhad is the same as the ancient one and lies at the southern end of the Druze Mountain, and because it is on the eastern border of the land of the Amorites it was fortified and strong (map 15).
The land taken includes all the cities of the plain, in addition to Gilead and all Bashan as far as the city of "Salchah" and the city of Edrei, which belonged to the kingdom of Og in Bashan.

Rabbath of the children of Ammon: the capital of the land of the children of Ammon, lying at the source of the Jabbok River, 35 km from the Jordan River; its modern name is Amman, and it is the capital of the Kingdom of Jordan (map 15). The Rephaims: a strong people who were contemporary with our father Abraham, and from whom strong peoples branched off.

Here he speaks of King Og as the last of the kings of the Rephaims, and describes his bedstead as about four and a half meters long and two meters wide, and it is in the city of "Rabbath of the children of Ammon." He mentions the great size of his bed to indicate the strength and great size of the body of this defeated king, who, whatever his bodily strength and the strength of his army, cannot overcome the divine power.

entries.section: (2) The distribution of the land and Moses' charge to them

paragraphs.text: Moses speaks here of the distribution of the land to some of the tribes of Israel. To the tribes of Reuben and Gad fell the region from "Aroer," which lies, as we mentioned before, in the valley of Arnon, the southern boundary of what the children of Israel possessed in the middle of the east of the Dead Sea (in whose south the Moabites dwell), to half of Mount Gilead and the cities of the mountain (ch. 2:36). God allowed Moses to enjoy seeing the lands they had possessed east of the Jordan, to gladden his heart, and likewise to look at the Promised Land west of the Jordan River, which they would possess after his death (map 15).

entries.section: (2) The distribution of the land and Moses' charge to them

paragraphs.text: Half the tribe of Manasseh possessed the rest of Gilead and all the region of Bashan, which formed the kingdom of Og, including the region of Argob, which is the province of Bashan, which anciently the tribe of the Rephaims inhabited, and which includes sixty fortified cities and lies east of the Sea of Galilee (maps 10, 15). We notice here the fulfillment of Jacob's prophecy to the two sons of Joseph, Ephraim and Manasseh (Gen 48:17-19), that the younger, Ephraim, would be blessed more than the firstborn, Manasseh; for the tribe of Manasseh was divided into two parts, the first half dwelling east of the Jordan and the other half west of the Jordan. As for Ephraim, he dwelt with all his clans in one place, and they were the largest of the tribes in number and had great strength.

entries.section: (2) The distribution of the land and Moses' charge to them

paragraphs.text: The Geshurites: the inhabitants of Geshur, a region lying between "Argob" on the east (v. 13) and the Sea of Galilee on the west.
The Maachathites: the people of Maachah, a small kingdom on the north-eastern border of Palestine, now called "Beit Jann," lying north of the Sea of Galilee.

Bashan-havoth-jair: a region in Bashan that was called the region of Argob until Jair, one of the clans of the tribe of Manasseh, took it and named it Bashan-havoth-jair, which means the villages or encampments of Jair.

The land that fell to the tribe of Manasseh was divided between two families in this tribe, the family of Machir and the family of Jair. Jair took all the region of Argob as far as its border with the regions of Geshur and Maachah, and changed the name of the region (that is, the district) and called it "Bashan-havoth-jair"; as for Machir, he took Gilead, which lies south of the river of Jair and east of the Jordan River and south of the Sea of Galilee.

entries.section: (2) The distribution of the land and Moses' charge to them

paragraphs.text: Chinnereth: a fortified city on the north-western bank of the Sea of Galilee, now called "Tell el-Azeimeh"; the lake is also called by its name, that is, the Sea of Chinnereth or Chinneroth, and it is the same as the Sea of Galilee or the Sea of Tiberias or the Lake of Gennesaret.
The sea of the plain (the Salt Sea): the same as the "Dead Sea," now also called the "Sea of Lot," south-east of Jerusalem.
Pisgah: part of the Abarim mountain range lying at the north-eastern end of the Dead Sea, on the southern border of the kingdom of Sihon, and now called "Ras el-Siyaghah."

He mentions here the boundaries of the lands which the tribes of Reuben and Gad and half the tribe of Manasseh possessed. Half the tribe of Manasseh dwelt in the north, that is, east of the Sea of Galilee and the Jordan River; then the tribe of Gad dwelt south of it, its lands bounded by the Jordan River on the west and the country of the children of Ammon on the east, and the Jabbok River, a tributary of the Jordan River, passes through the middle of its lands. Then the tribe of Reuben dwelt south of the tribe of Gad, bounded on the west by the Dead Sea, on the south by the Arnon River and the kingdom of Moab, and on the east by the kingdom of the children of Ammon, and the Abarim mountains and Ras Pisgah lie within its borders. The cities which these tribes possessed are mentioned in (Num 32:1-5, 34-42) (map 15).

entries.section: (2) The distribution of the land and Moses' charge to them

paragraphs.text: Armed: wearing the implements of war and ready for battle.
Before your brethren: you will share with the rest of the tribes in the war and go in front of them.
All that are meet for the war: that is, every one of you who has strength to fight.

Moses agreed to the request of the two tribes to settle and take their portion in the region east of the Jordan River, but on condition that they not leave the rest of the tribes to fight alone to obtain their portions in the Promised Land, which is west of the Jordan River, that is, the land of Canaan; rather they must go out to war with them until they achieve victory and possess the land, and only then could they return to their own (Num 32).

entries.section: (2) The distribution of the land and Moses' charge to them

paragraphs.text: He allowed them to leave their wives and children in the cities they had taken east of the Jordan, and likewise their many cattle, because of which they had asked to dwell in the land east of the Jordan, where there are many good pastures.

entries.section: (2) The distribution of the land and Moses' charge to them

paragraphs.text: Beyond the Jordan: this is applied to both the eastern and western banks of the river, and what is meant here is the western bank, where the rest of the tribes would take possession.

When victory is achieved for the rest of the tribes and they possess their portions in the Promised Land west of the Jordan, they could return to the regions in which they had previously settled east of the Jordan.

This teaches us not to live a selfish life in which we alone enjoy settled ease and quiet, where all our needs are supplied, without regard for the rest of our brethren who are in need spiritually and materially. Rather we must share the cares of those around us, feeling with them and showing our love for them and striving with them as members of one Church and one body, the Body of Christ, and offer our prayers for our brethren and help them, and not rest until we are assured of their passing out of the state of anxiety and need into spiritual and psychological fullness.

Since Moses knew that his departure from this world was near, he charged his successor Joshua always to keep in mind what the Lord had done for His people and His standing in their midst to give them victory over the two kings, Sihon and Og. He assures him that the Lord will do the same with them when they meet the other peoples dwelling in the land promised to them, which lies west of the Jordan. And he repeats the same warning to them which he had affirmed many times, that they should not fear meeting and fighting those peoples, because the Lord will give them victory over them.

Pay attention to the counsels of your elders and those with more experience than you; rather, may you seek to learn from everyone who is older than you in any field, for it is the distillation of their lives and it is the voice of God directed to you. Your independent character does not mean that you neglect the counsels of others, for this is a kind of pride that deprives you of many blessings.

entries.section: (4) The Lord does not allow Moses to cross over

paragraphs.text: At that time Moses beseeches God, after a short prayer in which he confesses to the Lord His greatness and power, which were clearly manifested in all the works He had done with His people, and that He, God, is the only God in heaven and on earth, and there is no other god who does the same works and has the same power.

entries.section: (4) The Lord does not allow Moses to cross over

paragraphs.text: The stubborn people were, as we learned before, the cause of the Lord's wrath against Moses and Aaron and of His refusal to grant his request; and the Lord's reply was as merciful as it was decisive, for He did not wish to deprive Moses entirely of seeing the land. Moses received many blessings throughout his life and fulfilled his mission faithfully, for which he deserved to enjoy blessed eternal life. The Lord fulfilled his desire in part by allowing him to see the land from afar, without entering it, so He asked him to go up a high mountain, the mountain of Pisgah, which lies at the north-eastern end of the Dead Sea (maps 6, 15), whose summit overlooks the wilderness, and whoever looks from its summit, called "Nebo," sees a large part of the land of Canaan west of the Jordan River; so Moses looked from it and saw the Promised Land (map 6).

entries.section: (4) The Lord does not allow Moses to cross over

paragraphs.text: The Lord asks him to charge his successor Joshua, to strengthen his heart and encourage him, because he is the one who will take over the leadership of the people after Moses and bring them into the land and divide it among their tribes. Here appear the submission of Moses and his obedience to God and his acceptance of His arrangements, for he rejoiced that Joshua would succeed him and declared this before all the people, like John the Baptist, who rejoiced to submit to Christ (Jn 3:29, 30).

entries.section: (4) The Lord does not allow Moses to cross over

paragraphs.text: The valley: the wide valley in which they encamped, in the plains of Moab, adjoining Ras Pisgah. Beth-peor: a city in the kingdom of Sihon opposite Mount Pisgah, the place where the Moabites worshipped their god Peor.
They stopped in the wide valley before the city of "Beth-peor"; that is, Moses remained with the people for a time and then went up to Ras Pisgah, and there he died after seeing the Promised Land.
May you submit to God's commandments and arrangements in your life, for they are the best thing for you even if they seem contrary to your desires ... He loves you more than you love yourself.
Encouragement to keep the commandments
Statutes: the duties which God commanded His people, relating to worship and rites.
Judgments: God's commandments concerning conduct and the various dealings.
Now therefore, O Israel: Moses declares the following words on the basis of the preceding events, which are:
1- God's care for His people in bringing them out of the land of Egypt and tending them in the wilderness of Sinai.
2- God's choosing them as a people of His own, so that they are bound to His commands.
3- Their preparation to enter the Promised Land to live in it in purity, instead of the evil and the wicked whom they will remove.
4- The nearness of Moses' departure from the world, so that he gives them the distillation of his experience, his fatherhood and his guidance.

Moses asked his people to listen attentively to God's commandments, which he would now confirm to them, that they might keep them and so be truly His children and deserve to enter the Promised Land; and God's commandments and word give them a life that is not only spiritual with God but also guides them in pure practical conduct in their dealings and all their works.

Moses warned them against adding any human ideas to God's commandments, however logical they may seem, because God's word is higher than all human speech. On the other side, no one should rush to remove any commandment he finds hard or unconvincing, for the weakness is in his own understanding and not in God's perfect word; that is, all of God's commandments must be kept. Christ affirmed the same meaning in His Sermon on the Mount (Mt 5:17, 18), and likewise the Book of Revelation affirmed the same meaning (Rev 22:18, 19).
Baal-peor: the name of a god of the Moabites, worshipped on Mount Peor, which is one of the peaks of the Abarim mountain range in the kingdom of Moab.

Moses reminded them of what happened when they fell into the sin of fornication and the worship of Peor, the pagan god of the Moabites, when Balak enticed them with the Moabite women, so God struck them with the plague and commanded that many of them be killed (Num 25). By this he warns them against turning away from God's commandments and against the worship of idols and evil lusts.

You who did cleave unto the Lord: those who hold fast to the Lord's commandments whatever enticements and lusts they face. Moses encourages those who hear him, who held fast to God's commandments and did not fall into fornication and idol worship at the pagan god Peor, and he praises them and reminds them of the grace of life that came as a result of their holding fast to God.

Moses warns them of the necessity of holding fast to God's commandments when they enter the Promised Land, for they are their guide in all their life; God had given them some commandments to be carried out in the Promised Land and not in the wilderness of Sinai, such as the Feast of Tabernacles, and what they should do if leprosy afflicted their houses ... etc.

Moses draws their attention to the fact that their holding fast to God's commandments will give them wisdom and distinction in all their conduct, which the nations around them in the Promised Land will notice, so that they see the loftiness of their worship and conduct and feel the greatness of their God who gave them these commandments.

Moses added that their carrying out the commandments will show God's work in them and His nearness to them and His care for them, and this is completely different from the pagan gods who are far from their peoples and cannot care for them or give them judgments and statutes like God's commandments.

Remember that you are the light of the world and the salt of the earth, so hold fast to God's word and apply His commandments, that you may not cause people to stumble by your sins, but draw them by your pure conduct to the love of God who is in you.

entries.section: (2) Remembering the receiving of the Ten Commandments at Horeb

paragraphs.text: Moses warns the people against forgetting what happened to them in the wilderness of Sinai when God gave them the commandments and the Law, because their dwelling among the nations in the land of Canaan and their preoccupation with building and farming might distract them from the most important thing, which is God's commandments. He also charges them to teach these commandments to their children and to tell them what happened at the receiving of the Law on the mountain. This is what the Church is concerned with in the New Testament, namely the handing down of the spiritual life from fathers to children and discipleship within the Church.

entries.section: (2) Remembering the receiving of the Ten Commandments at Horeb

paragraphs.text: Moses reminds them of the day on which God commanded him to gather the people before the mountain on which His glory appeared and on which Moses received the commandments and the Law. On that day the greatness of God appeared, and the people feared Him greatly.

entries.section: (2) Remembering the receiving of the Ten Commandments at Horeb

paragraphs.text: Burned: blazed.
The midst of heaven: the middle of the sky and its highest part.

The people drew near to the mountain, and God's glory appeared in mighty manifestations, namely the fire that blazed on the top of the mountain and the mist, darkness and cloud that surrounded the mountain, to declare God's power and the inability of men to know all that is in Him; for He is the Almighty who in His humility condescends to be in the midst of His people and teach them His commandments that they may live by them and not fear the gods of the pagan nations. The children of Israel who stood before Moses on this day were children and saw this sight. But in the New Testament God's appearing was in a meek and humble form when He became incarnate and declared His commandments in His Sermon on the Mount with simplicity and gentleness. This is the grace of the New Testament, for after we fear God we can enjoy His gentleness and tenderness.

entries.section: (2) Remembering the receiving of the Ten Commandments at Horeb

paragraphs.text: The people heard the voice of words when the Lord spoke to them, but saw no form, lest they afterwards make an image of the god and worship the image and forget the true God. The Lord forbade them repeatedly in His commandments to worship images or idols.

entries.section: (2) Remembering the receiving of the Ten Commandments at Horeb

paragraphs.text: The covenant here is the Ten Commandments written on two tablets of stone, which it expresses here as the ten words; and the stone tablets represent the document of the covenant that contains its conditions. The covenant is the basis of the relationship between God and His people, and obedience to these judgments represents the people's carrying out of the conditions, in return for God's care for them and their continued sonship to the living God.

entries.section: (2) Remembering the receiving of the Ten Commandments at Horeb

paragraphs.text: Moses assures them that the statutes and judgments which he taught them had God as their source, and that it was He who asked him to convey them to them after He had made them known to him. Moses warns them that they must apply these commandments and take them as principles governing their conduct when they take possession of the land to which they are crossing over, and hand them down from generation to generation, stressing the necessity of doing the commandment and not only teaching it. The Lord Christ said in the New Testament, "He who teaches and does," affirming the importance and necessity of doing what one teaches. It is also written in (Jas 2:18), "Shew me your faith without your works, and I will shew you my faith by my works."

Do not forget God's former works with you and your promises to Him, so that cares do not distract you from Him or problems disturb you, and let your relationship with God be the foundation of your daily life, so that you live in assurance.

Moses warns them against making images of God in order to worship them, for when God appeared to them on the mountain at Horeb to give them the commandments and the Law (Ex 19), He did not appear to them in any form or shape, but they heard only His voice, so it is not right for them to depict Him in an image of their own imagination.
Under the earth: because the level of the sea is lower than the land.

God gives them examples of the images which the pagan nations make, and warns them against making an image of Him, whether in the form of a man, male or female, or an animal, or a bird, or creeping things, or fish; all of these are creatures which God created to serve them, so how can they depict God by them and worship them, for God is higher than all these images.

Of course this is different from making icons of the saints to honor them in the Church, because the saints are created human beings with a definite form, and depicting them makes us remember them so that we ask for their intercession and honor them.
The host of heaven: the stars and planets.

Divided: God created them for the benefit of all mankind, and every person has a portion and share of them, that is, benefits from them. He also forbids them to depict Him in the form of one of the stars or planets which they see in the sky, for if their love and worship of God weaken they are dazzled by the greatness of these planets, so they depict God in one of their forms and bow down to them.

The nations' much gazing at the sun and the stars drew their hearts to them, so they worshipped them; therefore beware of gazing at and being preoccupied with the world, lest your heart be far from the love of God and you become carnal, seeking material things and forgetting God, but always remember that these material things are God's gifts offered to you, and thank Him.
The iron furnace: the crucible in which iron is smelted, whose temperature is very high, indeed the highest temperature known at that time ... and it signifies the severity of trials and sufferings.

A people of inheritance: a special people who worship God, and He gives them the Promised Land as an inheritance, which is a type of the Kingdom of Heaven; they are holy to God and God dwells among them and blesses them.

Moses reminds them of God's love for them, for He delivered them from the harsh bondage of Egypt with all its toils and the mingling with the pagans and their idols that went with it, so that they might live in the wilderness as a special people who worship Him alone, and He gives them the Promised Land, on the threshold of which they have now arrived.

Moses warns them of God's justice: just as He punished him personally by forbidding him to enter the Promised Land because of his disobedience to God in striking the rock twice at Kadesh (ch. 1:37), as a result of the people's murmuring and provoking him, so too He will punish severely everyone who disobeys His command by making images to worship them. This is the third time that Moses declares God's prohibition against his entering the Promised Land (ch. 1:37; ch. 3:26, 27), and this shows how bitter his heart was because of his longing to see God's love and the Promised Land, which is a type of the eternal Kingdom.

Thus Moses will die on the eastern bank of the Jordan River, and the children of Israel will cross over and possess the land of Canaan. This is God's punishment of Moses, and at the same time he warns them to hold fast to God's commandments and not to worship idols after his death and their entering the Promised Land and dwelling among the pagan peoples who worship images.
He repeats his warning to them against making images, lest they be punished by God.
Moses shows the power of God's justice, likening Him to a consuming fire, that is, one that destroys everyone who persists in disobeying Him.

He also points to God's intense love for His people, likening it to the love of a bridegroom for his bride, for whom he is jealous over her inclination to any other man besides him, so that he takes vengeance on her and on him; so too God is a jealous God who punishes His people severely if they leave Him and worship another god besides Him, especially after all the love and care they have received from Him, for their rest and good are in worshipping Him and living with Him.

Moses also warns them that after their settling in the land of Canaan for many years and the birth of children and grandchildren, they may forget God's commandments and imitate the pagan nations around them, making images like them and worshipping them, because a person's material settledness very often invites him to laxity, so that he neglects the worship of God.
Heaven and earth: what is meant is the inanimate creatures obedient to God, and also those in them, the angels in heaven and men on earth.

God testifies against them that if they disobey His commandments and worship idols, they will perish and be driven from this land, because it is God's gift to them; if they do not obey Him, He will take it from them and remove them from it.

God threatens them that they will be scattered among the nations of the earth and their numbers will dwindle, so that they become a small people of no value among the peoples of the earth, and this is what happened during the captivity.
In the places to which God will drive them they will live among the pagans, so they will sink down like them and make lifeless images and, sadly, worship them.

It appears here that Moses' warnings to them include details which he knew by the spirit of prophecy, so he warns his people in the hope that they will take heed and hold fast to God's commandments and His worship.

entries.section: (4) There is none other besides God

paragraphs.text: God's tenderness toward His people appears in that, although they fell into the worship of idols and were punished with captivity and driven from their land to scattered places in the world, yet if they repent there and seek God, He forgives them and they find help from Him that supports them and rescues them from captivity. But the condition is that the repentance be with all the heart and the seeking of God with complete faith, that is, refusing to rely on pagan gods and all the powers of the world.

entries.section: (4) There is none other besides God

paragraphs.text: When thou art in tribulation: God punished you with captivity and driving out from your land to other, foreign countries.
The latter days: after the completion of the punishment by captivity.

God allows His people to be disciplined for a full period, which is the period of the captivity, and at its end the people feel their error and repent, and God receives them, and their inner senses are opened and they care to hear God's commandments and worship Him faithfully, so He has mercy on them and removes from them all discipline. It also means that in the latter days, that is, in the fullness of time, God's mercy appears in the incarnation of Christ to redeem His people and everyone who believes in Him.

entries.section: (4) There is none other besides God

paragraphs.text: He affirms here God's mercy, which appears in His holding fast to His covenant with His people, which He gave to the fathers "Abraham, Isaac and Jacob" by blessing their descendants, so He forgives them their sins and brings them back from captivity to their country, as happened at the hands of Zerubbabel, Ezra and Nehemiah (Ezra 1, 2; Neh 7, 8) and as happened by the incarnation of Christ.

entries.section: (4) There is none other besides God

paragraphs.text: The days that are past: from the creation of the world.
From the one side of heaven unto the other: that is, every place on earth, from east to west and from north to south.

Moses shows God's care for His people, which has not happened with any other people in the world, and God draws His people's attention to ponder it, for it has not happened with any people since the creation of the world and in every place on earth.

entries.section: (4) There is none other besides God

paragraphs.text: He reminds them of God's grace that appeared in His speaking with them from the mountain, when He gave Moses the commandments and the Law and appeared in the form of a great fire on the mountain, yet it did not burn the people and they did not die because of the greatness of God's voice, but enjoyed, unlike the other peoples of the earth, hearing His voice and rejoicing in His care.

entries.section: (4) There is none other besides God

paragraphs.text: He declares another manifestation of God's care, which is His choosing them as a special people for Himself and bringing them out from the midst of a great nation, the people of Egypt, which was reckoned the strongest of peoples at that time, and this by a great divine power which appeared in the ten plagues and then the crossing of the Red Sea and the destruction of the Egyptians.

entries.section: (4) There is none other besides God

paragraphs.text: The people of God saw with their own eyes all that God did with them in Egypt and in the wilderness of Sinai, and these wonders declare that He is the only God and that all the gods of the pagan nations are demons.

entries.section: (4) There is none other besides God

paragraphs.text: The purpose of hearing God's voice is to plant His fear in the heart of His people, which was also manifested in seeing Him in His great fire on the mountain in Sinai; for God's voice and seeing Him in the fire declare that He is the only God, who loves His people and shepherds them.

entries.section: (4) There is none other besides God

paragraphs.text: In His sight: Himself, by means of His dwelling in the midst of His people.

God's love appeared in His holding fast to His promises to the fathers Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, so He delivered their descendants, that is, His people, from the bondage of Egypt by means of the ten plagues, and led them by the pillar of cloud and the pillar of fire, which declares His dwelling in their midst, and took them through the Red Sea and drowned Pharaoh and all his army.

entries.section: (4) There is none other besides God

paragraphs.text: After their departure from Egypt God also led them to victory over peoples stronger than they, so He drove out kings before them, such as Sihon king of Heshbon and Og king of Bashan (ch. 2, 3), and gave the land of these kings to two and a half of their tribes. Indeed He will also drive out the Canaanites from the western bank of the Jordan River and give their land to the rest of the tribes of Israel.

entries.section: (4) There is none other besides God

paragraphs.text: The final result of all the foregoing is the confidence of God's people in Him that He is the only God in heaven and on earth, and that everything the pagans claim as gods in heaven or on earth are demons, and the people of God must repeat this faith in order to establish it in their hearts.

Repeating the Psalms and verses reminds us of God's presence with us, so it gives reassurance to our hearts and also gives us His fear, so we guard against sin and keep far from it, and if we sin we repent quickly.

entries.section: (4) There is none other besides God

paragraphs.text: As a result of faith in the one God and in His great power, love and care for His people, His children must hold fast to His commandments and laws throughout their lives, and God will keep them and their children in peace and give them a long life and an enjoyment of their days with God that extends into eternity by their being with Him in the Kingdom of Heaven.
On this side Jordan toward the sunrising: on the eastern bank of the Jordan River.
Bezer: it lies about 30 km north-east of the Dead Sea.
Ramoth in Gilead: it lies about 45 km east of the Sea of Galilee.
Golan: north-east of the Sea of Galilee (map 11).
