May you be considerate of people's feelings when you deal with them, especially when you give them responsibilities to carry out, and support them with your encouragement, so that you may reap good results from their work.

In this verse, and up to (v. 15), he speaks of the case of fighting against a distant city, while in (vv. 16-18) he speaks of the case of fighting against a city in the Promised Land. In the first case, the first thing to be done is to summon that city to peace, that is, to invite it to make a treaty. God commands this because, if these distant cities were left alone, they might fight against them, so it is necessary to subdue them and put their men to forced labor.

If the city responds to the call to peace, the sentence of annihilation is not applied to its inhabitants, but they become servants of Israel, and Israel puts them to work in farming and building. Many of them converted to Judaism and gained rights like the rest of the Jews because of the good treatment the Jews showed them.
But if that city refuses the offer of peace and prepares for war against you, then you must lay siege to it.

When God gives you victory over it, kill all its males with the sword, but the women, the children, the animals, and the rest of the spoil found in the city, whether money or possessions, you shall take for yourselves. This is as happened in the killing of the Midianites in the days of Moses (Num 31:25-30), and of Ai in the days of Joshua (Josh 8:2). The spoil is considered a reward that the Lord appointed for them as payment for their participation in holy wars, which are the wars of the Lord.

The Lord laid down this conduct for them in the case of war with a distant nation, not one of the Canaanite nations dwelling in the Promised Land, because the distant cities, by reason of their distance, posed no danger to their spiritual life.

Give an opportunity for understanding with those around you, so that you may save much effort and reach your goals quickly. Do not rush into thinking evil of others and so sin against them and against God.

entries.section: (4) The annihilation of the pagans and of the trees

paragraphs.text: As for the peoples of the land, under their various names, who dwell in the cities within the bounds of the Promised Land, they are to be placed under the ban completely, that is, all their inhabitants are to be destroyed according to the Lord's command, in order to be rid of idol worship and evil lusts, so that the people of God may live in purity. The reason here is the destruction of evil, not hatred, whereas in the New Testament, after faith has been established, God requires us to love our enemies.

entries.section: (4) The annihilation of the pagans and of the trees

paragraphs.text: Allowing these peoples to remain carried the danger of their influencing the people of Israel, enticing them to their idolatrous worship of their gods, with the defilements contained in the rituals of those cults and the rebellion against the true God that they involve, so that the people would sin against the Lord.

entries.section: (4) The annihilation of the pagans and of the trees

paragraphs.text: While you are besieging a certain city, before you enter that city and take it, if you find trees that bear edible fruit, do not cut them down, because they are needed for your food, and cutting them down would be the loss of something important and necessary for human life. Moreover, these trees pose no danger to you: they are not men who could resist you in the siege, nor is there fear that they would turn back with a new war against you, nor will they harm you spiritually.

entries.section: (4) The annihilation of the pagans and of the trees

paragraphs.text: But the other, unfruitful trees you may cut down and use their wood for the siegeworks necessary for besieging cities, until their people surrender to you.
Cut off every cause of evil, however dear it may be in your eyes, so that you may live purely and give the devil no opportunity to fight you through it.
The unknown murderer, the marriage of the captive woman, the treatment of sons, and the crucified

Murder is one of the gravest sins forbidden by the Ten Commandments (Ex 20:12), and it carries a severe penalty in the case of deliberate murder (ch. 19). But if the body of a slain man is found in the field and it is not known who killed him, what are they to do? This is what he will explain in the following verses.

A group of the elders and judges of the people is chosen to measure the distance from the place where the body was found to the surrounding cities, in order to determine the city nearest to the scene, since it is most likely that the murderer was from that city.
Yoke: the piece of wood placed on the neck of the animal that pulls the plow or turns the waterwheel.
After the nearest city is determined, it becomes the duty of its elders to bring a heifer of the herd that has not yet been used in any farm work and has not been placed under a yoke.

In the rest of the ritual this heifer will be slaughtered, as a symbolic carrying out of the death penalty that ought to be carried out on the unknown murderer. Therefore the condition that it had never been used before points to the person of the murderer, who is of no use to his society and his people, and from whom no good work comes.

They take the heifer and bring it to a valley with a flowing stream of water, which has not been plowed or sown by anyone, and they slaughter it there. The valley that has not been plowed or sown by anyone also points to the murderer, from whom nothing useful is expected, and the flowing stream of water points to the washing away of sin and forgiveness for the people of the city.

The priests, the sons of Levi, must be present to supervise the ritual described, because the Lord has chosen them as stewards of the Law and its application, and to bless the people, and according to what they judge, every case, dispute, or disagreement between members of the people is decided, as well as any assault by one person on another, such as beating or killing.

Washing the hands is an act that symbolizes a declaration of the innocence from guilt of the one who washes his hands in a particular situation. Something like this was done by Pontius Pilate when he pronounced the sentence of the crucifixion of Christ, and it is done by the priest in the Divine Liturgy to declare his innocence of responsibility for whoever approaches Communion unworthily. This symbolic act is also performed in the setting out of this ritual, since the elders of the nearest city, after slaughtering the heifer, must wash their hands over it as a sign of their innocence of the blood of the slain man.
The washing of the hands is accompanied by their declaration in a loud voice that they have not come to know the offender and did not see the murder as it was happening.

Then they turn in prayer to God, asking forgiveness and entreating Him not to lay upon them the responsibility for the blood of the one who was killed, remembering that they are the people whom the Lord acquired and delivered from the bondage of Pharaoh. When this ritual is followed in full, the Lord answers the prayer of the elders and forgives His people, and the charge of shedding the blood of the slain man is not laid upon the people of the city.
What is right in the eyes of the Lord: carrying out the ritual, as well as God's commandments.

If you carry out what the Lord commanded of ritual for this event, and your conduct is according to the Lord's commandments and in keeping with His Law, the responsibility for shedding this blood will not fall on you.
If you see anything wrong, do not be hasty in judging and thinking evil of others, but ask God to forgive the one who erred and to help him, or to help the one to whom harm has happened.

entries.section: (2) The marriage of the captive woman

paragraphs.text: Verses (10:14) speak of the conduct toward the women who are taken captive in one of the wars. The Lord commanded them to treat prisoners and captives well, and these are from the peoples whom God did not command to be placed under the ban, that is, to have everyone in them killed, as with the Canaanite peoples.

entries.section: (2) The marriage of the captive woman

paragraphs.text: If one of the victorious warriors, or one of the people, sees a woman among the captives and is pleased with her beauty, so that his heart is attached to her and he wants to marry her, he must apply the Law that the Lord dictates to him in the following verses.

entries.section: (2) The marriage of the captive woman

paragraphs.text: He must take her to his house, shave her head, and trim her nails. These two customs were among the signs of grief and mourning, and this means giving her an opportunity to grieve for those she has been parted from, family, relatives, and loved ones.

entries.section: (2) The marriage of the captive woman

paragraphs.text: He changes her clothes: instead of the clothes she was accustomed to wear, which may have had a special appearance connected with idol worship, he gives her clothes suitable for the people of God, and she remains in his house mourning her father and mother for a full month, and after that he marries her. Her remaining in his house a month before the marriage is for the following reasons:
1- An opportunity for her feelings to calm because of her deprivation of her family and her country; it is a kind of gentleness and compassion and respect for her feelings.
2- An opportunity for her to learn faith in God and His worship.
3- So that she may forget idol worship and all the customs connected with it.
4- So that the new husband may be certain of his feelings toward her, for it is like a period of engagement.

entries.section: (2) The marriage of the captive woman

paragraphs.text: Enslave her: from servitude, that is, to make her a slave girl.

If it happens that after a period of marriage the husband no longer wishes to continue living with her, the Lord has set down a text in His Law to protect her, and does not allow her to be mistreated or exploited. He must set her free, and the Law does not permit him to sell her as a slave girl, because she had been his lawful wife in fact, so it is not right for him to take her as a slave girl. Releasing her as a free woman is compensation to her for his change of mind about remaining with her as a wife, and it is enough that he has grieved and humiliated her by divorcing her.

May you be considerate of the feelings of those around you, especially those to whom you have done wrong; you must apologize to them, and even compensate them for any harm that befell them because of you.

The following text protects the rights of the firstborn son of a man married to more than one wife, and it addresses the question of discrimination among children. Suppose a man is married to two women and prefers one to the other, and he has children by both of them, but the firstborn son is from the wife whom he loves less than the other.

When he divides his property among them or writes his will, it is not lawful for him to deprive the firstborn son of the hated wife of the right of the firstborn and give it to another son among the sons of the beloved wife. And if Jacob honored Joseph and made him the firstborn (Gen 48:22), it was not because he was the son of Rachel the beloved, but for his faithfulness, obedience, and service to his father and brothers more than the rest of his sons, whereas Reuben the firstborn lost his birthright because he lay with his father's wife (Gen 35:22).

Rather, he must understand and acknowledge that the son of the wife who is less favored by him is the firstborn, and he must give him the right of the firstborn, a double portion of his property, because he is the first fruit of his strength, whom he begot in the prime of his power. A double portion: that is, twice the share of any of his brothers.
Rebellious: defiant.

The commandment here speaks of the disobedient son who does not listen to the voice of his father or the voice of his mother, while they try to discipline him and correct his conduct, but he refuses advice and does not submit to them.
The gate of his place: the gate of the city.

The parents must then take him to the elders of the city who are responsible for examining matters that threaten order and the family, to where they usually gather at the gate of the city, which is the place designated for holding trials.

The parents complain to the judges about their son, that he is a disobedient son who defies them, does not obey them, and does not listen to their advice, and in addition to that he is a spendthrift and a drunkard; that is, they state his evil deeds, which are considered a danger to society and the family. This of course does not happen with any parents except when they are unable to correct the behavior of their son.

The judgment of the Law on such a disobedient son was stoning to death, and thus the doers of evil are removed from among the holy people, and others hear of this sentence, so that matters are set right and what is crooked is straightened, through the sons' fear that their disobedience might bring them to such an end.

If stubbornness toward parents deserves the sentence of death, what then would be the sentence for stubbornness toward God Himself? Many among us resist the Lord's call to them and linger in returning to the bosom of the Church, our mother. Let us take heed before it is too late and we lose our worthiness as sons and heirs of the Kingdom.
In the case of carrying out the death sentence on any person and killing him, and afterward hanging his body on a tree, the following must be observed, as stated in the next verse.

It is noted that execution among the Jews was not by crucifixion as with the Romans, but he was first put to death in some way, such as stoning, and then his body was hanged on a tree, that is, crucified, in order to publicize his sin so that people would fear and not sin as he did.

The Law requires that he not be left hanging on the wood of the cross until the next day, but that he must be taken down from the cross and buried on the same day (which was what was done in the crucifixion of our Lord Jesus Christ). The wisdom in this is that man is created in the image of God, so the exposure of him must not be prolonged; the exposure of his sin has been sufficient on the same day. And the body's remaining hanging means the continued proclamation of the crime connected with it, which made the one hanged accursed of God, that is, under His wrath, because he broke His Law and dared the heinous deed for which he deserved this sentence. Also, the Law's insistence on the necessity of burying the body on the same day is because God does not want our fear of our sins to dominate our thinking for long, as long as the body remains hanging, rebuking us; rather, He asks us to repent of them and to occupy our thoughts with God as the forgiver of sins and not as our judge; in addition, bodies that are not buried spread diseases.
That you defile not your land which the Lord your God gives you for an inheritance: the bodies of the slain were considered an uncleanness that defiled the land, so they had to be buried quickly.

How great is God's love for us in sending His beloved Son to redeem us from the curse of the Law, being made a curse for us, for it is written, "Cursed is every one that hangeth on a tree" (Gal 3:13). He Himself bore our sins in His body on the tree, that we, being dead to sins, should live unto righteousness. Let us therefore come with confidence to the throne of grace, offering true repentance, assured of its acceptance, believing in Him who redeemed us and opened for us the way to the Kingdom, meditating on the saying of the Apostle Paul: "Every transgression and disobedience received a just recompence of reward; how shall we escape, if we neglect so great salvation" (Heb 2:2, 3). Compassion, mixing, and adultery
In any case: without doubt or hesitation.

The Law highlights the importance of mercy in returning a stray ox or sheep to its owner if he is one of the Jews. The Book of Exodus (Ex 23:4) mentions returning a stray animal to an enemy; and in the New Testament, in the parable of the Good Samaritan, Christ showed that the neighbor is every human being (Lk 10:30-36).
If you do not know the owner of the stray animal, keep it in your house until its owner seeks it, and then you give it to him.

In any similar circumstance in which a neighbor or relative loses some of his possessions, such as one of his animals or his garment or anything else, you must do what you can to return the lost thing to its owner, and not neglect it.

The Law requires helping any Jew whose ox or donkey has fallen under its load, so that he can continue on his way. The Book of Exodus also commanded helping an enemy if his ox or donkey has fallen under its load (Ex 23:5).

God desires by this commandment that each person behave according to the nature with which God created him. If a woman puts on a man's clothes, she may forget her gentleness and behave roughly like a man; likewise, a man who puts on a woman's clothes may incline toward effeminacy. So both man and woman must observe modesty in their dress and not depart from custom and moderation, and this also resists the habit of sexual perversion.

If you happen upon a bird's nest on the way, in a tree or on the ground, with the mother sitting on her eggs or her young, it is not lawful for you to take both the mother and the young, but you must take only the young for yourself and let the mother go.

This legislation shows the extent of the Lord's care for all His creation, even the birds, and it also shows the importance of the mother and the appreciation of her role in preserving the species, for it is the mother who brings forth the eggs and not the reverse.

The reward announced for carrying out this commandment reminds us of the fifth commandment, which orders the honoring of parents in (Ex 20:12), "that thy days may be long upon the land." While the Jews considered the commandment concerning birds to be the least of the commandments in the Law, the Lord affirms the high standing of motherhood in the world of animals and birds as in the world of men, that is, His sanctification of motherhood in all its forms.

The roofs of houses in the East are flat, and they were used for many purposes, among them sitting in the winter sun and sleeping in the summer to enjoy the pleasant air; guests were also received on them, and they were used for storing some things, and so on. So Moses commands the owner of the house to build a parapet for the roof, so that no one falls from it by accident and the owner of the house be held responsible for the blood of the one who fell. The wisdom of this commandment is that a person must not expose his brother to harm, but must take everything necessary to preserve the lives of others, for the Lord cares for the lives and safety of people.

The spirit of love and compassion for others will extend spontaneously to compassion for animals and plants. So be merciful to all, that you may obtain God's mercies. Put yourself in the place of everyone before you deal with him, so that you may feel with him, make excuses for him, and be tender toward him.
The fullness ("seed"): everything that has been sown.

What is meant here is not sowing two different kinds of grain at one time in the same field. Naturally, each kind has its own system, different from the other, in irrigation and care, so that it may grow and be harvested at its own time, which may differ from the other's.

Lest the fullness be defiled ("sanctified"): meaning that everything that has been sown is subject to the application of the law of the firstfruits and the tithes for each kind separately, that is, he offers the firstfruits of each kind and the tithes of each kind, which may confuse the owner of the field and expose him to error and shortcoming in the Lord's rights. This is also a symbol of undesirable mixing with the wicked. This law was mentioned in (Lev 19:19).

You shall not yoke an ox and a donkey together under one yoke, because the ox is stronger than the donkey, and therefore the donkey cannot keep up with the ox in the length of its stride and its endurance, so the donkey is exhausted. It is well known that the ox is among the clean animals in the Law, while the donkey is among the unclean.

In this is a warning to the believer not to assign two people who differ in ability and gifts to do the same work, but to ask of each one what suits his mental, physical, and health capacities. Likewise, spiritually, believers are not to mix with unbelievers, in application of the Apostle's saying in (2 Cor 6:14), lest they become like them and share with them in their evil works.

Wool and linen each have natural properties that differ from one another, so the life of a garment woven from a mixture of the two is determined by the life of the kind that wears out faster, which causes the loss of the whole garment. Spiritually, the people of God must be distinguished by purity and be one fabric, with one spirit and one mind.

We note here that verses (9-11) are all symbolic images urging us not to mix contradictory things, and calling us to acquire the spirit of discernment between divine truth and the falsehood of the world, between purity and uncleanness, between holiness and license, between uprightness and deviation.
Be careful that concern for God and for the world do not mix in your heart, but let your whole heart be God's, and then use the world as a gift from God and do not cling to it for its own sake.
Tassels: threads that hang from the corners of the garment.

The purpose of this commandment is to distinguish the outward appearance of the Lord's people from the other peoples, so that the believer may be distinguished in his conduct and behavior from the people of the world, because clothes symbolize conduct.

If a man marries a young woman and, after having relations with her, hates her and accuses her of not having been a virgin before the marriage, whether this is a true accusation, that is, he did not find in her the sign proving that she was a virgin, or his accusation was false and he claimed it because of his hatred of her.

The young woman's parents bring the case before the elders of the city, who undertake the judging in the court, whose seat is at the gate of the city (as a place known to everyone), and they present to them the sign of their daughter's virginity that appeared on the day of her marriage, since the family of the bride in the East, and in some places even now, took care to keep this sign to prove her virginity before marriage; but with the progress of civilization this custom has faded, out of consideration for the bride's feelings and her modesty.

The parents declare before the judges that the husband hated their daughter and that this is the reason he spread his false rumor that she was not a virgin, and here is the sign of virginity presented before them, which is their daughter's garment bearing the sign of her virginity.

The judges, on the basis of the evidence presented which proves the innocence of the young woman, rule that the husband be disciplined in some way (beating, rebuke, or otherwise)... and as compensation to the young woman whose innocence has been proved and whose reputation has been restored, they rule that the husband be fined one hundred shekels of silver, which he pays to the young woman's father. This is considered a ruling that the family's reputation is sound, and this fine is double the dowry that is paid at marriage (v. 28).
Here the commandment addresses another case, which is that the charge is proved against the young woman and the husband was truthful in his claim against her.

The judges bring her to the door of her father's house, as an indication of that house's failure in raising the daughter and the father's negligence in watching over her conduct, which caused the young woman's deviation and her committing a vile transgression unbecoming to the daughters of the holy people while she was still in her father's house, and she is stoned there to death. By this sentence, by which they are rid of this young woman, they will have put away evil from their midst.

Adultery with a married woman is a crime in the Jewish Law, and its penalty is the stoning to death of the man and the woman: the man is stoned here because he violated his brother's honor, and the woman because she betrayed her husband (Lev 20:10).

In the case of a man committing adultery with a betrothed young woman, who is considered in the position of a married woman, as the Virgin and Joseph the carpenter were (Mt 1:20,) and this adultery takes place inside a populated city, both are sentenced to stoning: the man because he violated his brother's honor, and the young woman because she did not cry out for help to the people, which means that she consented to this adultery.

In the case of a man committing adultery with a betrothed young woman in the field, that is, in a place far from people, if the young woman cries out no one will hear her, so they stone the man, but for the young woman they find an excuse, because the man took advantage of her physical weakness, just as a man falls upon his brother in the field and kills him and he has no chance to call on anyone for help.

In the case of the discovery that a man has assaulted a virgin young woman who is not betrothed, the Law rules in this case that the man pay her father fifty (shekels) of silver (which is the same sum paid as a dowry for a wife). He must marry her because he assaulted her, and he cannot divorce her afterward all his life. But if her father refuses his marrying his daughter, he does not marry her; this is the young woman's right, but there is no compulsion on her to marry the one who assaulted her (Ex 22:16, 17).
His father's skirt: the skirt is the edge of the garment, and his father's skirt means that he lifted the garments of his father's wife and assaulted her in adultery.
It is not permissible for a son to marry his father's wife in any circumstances, whether during his father's lifetime if he has divorced her, or after his death when she has become a widow.

So when Reuben committed adultery with his father Jacob's wife, he was deprived of the birthright (Gen 48:22), and when Absalom assaulted the concubines of his father David, he died a shameful death in the war (2 Sam 16:22, 18:14, 15), and as a son in Corinth assaulted his father's wife, St. Paul the Apostle put him out of the Church for a time (1 Cor 5:
Be chaste in refusing any evil look, and reject every wicked thought, so that you may live in purity with everyone, and God will bless you and everyone will be at ease with you.
The purity of the people, vows, and the freedom and property of others

entries.section: (1) The admission of peoples into the assembly of the Lord

paragraphs.text: One emasculated by crushing: one who is castrated by crushing his testicles with a piece of stone or the like.
One mutilated: one who is castrated by cutting off the testicles with a sharp instrument.
The assembly of the Lord: the people of Israel, who entered into a covenant with the Lord that binds them to specific regulations, acts of worship, and rituals.

The purpose of this commandment is to prevent the castration of some persons for the purpose of dedicating them to service, as the pagans used to do, whether in their pagan temples or in the palaces of their kings, especially for serving the women, thinking that this is a kind of worship that pleases their gods. The Law excluded the eunuch from membership in the assembly of the Lord. For the Lord wanted His people not to imitate the pagans in their perverse deeds, and He also wanted to affirm to His people the sanctity of all the members of the body and to change the view of the sexual organs as defiled members.

And exclusion from membership means exclusion from enjoying full rights; they are not prevented from worshipping the Lord, but such a person is barred from practicing certain spiritual or leadership functions, such as the priesthood or being one of the leaders of the people.

entries.section: (1) The admission of peoples into the assembly of the Lord

paragraphs.text: Even to the tenth generation: this is a long time, meaning throughout the generations, and in another expression, not even after the tenth generation.

The son born as a result of an adulterous relationship is considered excluded from entering the assembly of the Lord. They are deprived of some rights, but this does not prevent any of them from worshipping God and having a place in eternal life, because he is not at fault.
The Lord established this for the following reasons:
1- So that the people would hate the sin of adultery, which is an uncleanness.
2- This son might also regard adultery as permissible and so spread this sin.
Some of them did attain a position of leadership, such as Jephthah the Gileadite (Judg 11:1-29).

entries.section: (1) The admission of peoples into the assembly of the Lord

paragraphs.text: Ammonite or Moabite: they are the descendants of Lot (Gen 19:37, 38). The Lord forbade any Ammonite or Moabite to enter the assembly of the Lord. The reason for the prohibition is what they did toward their cousins, the children of Israel, in the story of the Exodus from Egypt. For they did not supply them with their need of bread and water, whether by honoring them as guests and cousins, nor did they even agree to sell to them for a price. In addition, they summoned Balaam the son of Beor to curse them (Num 22, 23, 24). Nehemiah carried this out by excluding Tobiah the Ammonite and not dealing with him (Neh 13:7, 8). This means that the Moabites and the Ammonites were marked by two evil traits:
1- Harshness in their treatment of the children of Israel.
2- Hatred and revenge, as appeared in the matter of Balaam.

So the purpose of excluding them was their insistence on harming the children of Israel, but whoever believes in God and wants to join His people is accepted, like Ruth the Moabitess, who not only joined the people of God but became a grandmother of Christ.

entries.section: (1) The admission of peoples into the assembly of the Lord

paragraphs.text: The attempts of the Moabites to curse the holy people through Balaam did not succeed, because the Lord turned the curse into a blessing out of love for His people whom He had acquired for Himself.

entries.section: (1) The admission of peoples into the assembly of the Lord

paragraphs.text: God forbade them to make a peace treaty with them or to try to benefit from their good things, but to keep away from them all their lives because they persist in evil, so that they would not be defiled by the worship of their idols.

entries.section: (1) The admission of peoples into the assembly of the Lord

paragraphs.text: The Edomites are the descendants of Esau, the brother of Jacob, so they and the children of Israel are brothers; therefore the Lord commands them not to hate them.

Likewise the Egyptians, for they dwelt for a time in their land and enjoyed their good things, and they received them as guests and overwhelmed them with their generosity and kindness in the days of Joseph; therefore those of them who live as resident aliens in Israel may be accepted into the assembly of the Lord in the third generation only, and are not rejected forever as is the case with the Ammonites and Moabites, that is, the Edomite himself is not accepted, but the third generation of the Edomite married to the Jews, and the third generation means the children of the grandchildren. This makes clear that God keeps them away from certain peoples because of their abundant evil, such as Moab and the children of Ammon, but they love the Gentiles, with caution against the worship of idols and evil lusts; therefore they admit the third generation, which has been purified by the knowledge of God, so that it can worship Him and become a member of the assembly of God. And even the wicked, such as the Moabites, they do not treat as enemies but only separate themselves from them (ch. 2:9, 19).

Have love toward all the people around you, however wrongdoing and wicked they may be, but beware of excessive mixing with them, lest you be defiled by their strange thoughts and evil ways, and be careful, you and your sons and your grandsons, but teach your children to love everyone and to pray for everyone.
Wicked ("evil"): unclean.
He commands them that the warriors be committed to purity and keep away from everything unclean.
What chances by night: a nocturnal emission, that is, the discharge of seminal fluid.
The camp: the encampment, that is, the place where the warriors stay.
If one of the men has a nocturnal emission while sleeping, in the morning he goes outside the camp and stays there until evening, then he washes and is purified and enters the camp.

The second thing that the children of Israel observe is going outside the camp in order to dispose of their waste, so they designate a place for this, and the man goes out with a peg and digs a hole to relieve himself, then covers the excrement with earth.

The Lord explains the reason for the commandment concerning the two previous matters, which is the presence of God in the midst of His host, in order to fight for them and defeat their enemies. Therefore the camp must be pure and holy, lest God see in it something filthy that defiles the state of purity, and He leave them and not be in their midst.
And the observance of outward cleanliness points to inward purity and encourages its observance, for it constantly reminds them that they are a holy people, pure spiritually as they are bodily.
May you prepare for the Divine Liturgy with repentance, prayers, and purity of body, because you will meet God and be united with Him.
Escaped to you: has fled to you.
In one of your gates: in one of your cities.

The servant who suffered from the mistreatment of his master, whether from the people of Israel or from other peoples, and fled from him and took refuge with you seeking protection, it is not right for you to return him to his master, but you allow him to dwell among you in the place he chooses and in the city where he asks to stay, and you shall not oppress him, but treat him well as one of you, even if this servant is a pagan or from an enemy people.
This law protects the servant from exploitation, torture, and killing if his master catches him, as was customary among the ancient peoples.
And it is not understood from this commandment that a runaway servant is to be helped if he has committed a crime, but in this case he should be tried and held accountable.

Nor is it understood that the runaway servant is to be exploited to be a servant among the Jews, but they accept him as one wronged and give him a place to live as a human being, because the Law states that everything lost is to be returned to its owner (Ex 23:4). And by this commandment God implicitly resists the slavery that prevailed at that time, and so helps to free the wronged servant.
Be merciful and hasten to the aid of everyone who cries out to you, and help him and have compassion on him even if he wronged you before, for this is your opportunity to show him the love of Christ.
Sodomite: effeminate, sexually perverse, that is, one with whom a male has relations, treating him as in the place of a female.
Dog: the sodomite.
God forbids His people adultery and sexual perversion, and God does not accept a vow offered to Him in His house that comes from the wages of adultery or sexual perversion.
Be careful and keep away from evil sights, wicked company, and all places that cause you to stumble, so that you may be His son and worship Him in purity.

The Lord forbids the members of His people to lend to one another by taking interest (usury) on these loans, whether lending money, food, or anything else. As for lending to pagan foreigners, they may lend to them while collecting interest on those loans (Ex 22:25). For the members of the people among themselves, they had to live in a spirit of fellowship, because all that they have is a divine gift to them all, for they are one family, in addition to the fact that the one who borrows faces difficult circumstances, so it is not right to exploit the need of the brethren to make a profit. As for foreigners, collecting interest on loans was a practice in force among them and followed in their laws, so this is not new to them. But for the people of God it is a special privilege of theirs, which makes them feel sympathy, spiritual brotherhood, and mutual support among themselves.

Have compassion on those in financial distress, lend to them and do not take interest; indeed, may you not demand repayment of their debts either, and consider that part of your tithes and gifts, because it is God who blessed you and gave you everything you have, so do not be harsh on debtors. But if your heart doubts the need of the one who asks of you, give only a little, so that you will not be troubled if he does not repay you.

A person who makes a vow to the Lord must not delay fulfilling it, because the Lord is required to carry it out, so any delay or refusal to fulfill the vow is counted by the Lord as sin against him. Therefore haste in uttering a vow is not advisable, but the matter is taken with all seriousness.

The Lord obliges no one to vow. Individuals have complete freedom to vow or not to vow. If someone vows, let him do so with all love and all determination to fulfill it, not out of compulsion but with love and gratitude. And if he refrains from vowing at the outset, there is no sin on him, for the Lord does not need vows.

Everything a person promises in his vow, he becomes bound to fulfill exactly as he promised, that is, in the same measure and form in which he vowed. The offering is a voluntary offering that no one forced him to make.

God rejoices in your gifts because they are proof of your love, and He answers your requests because you are His child; but if you are unable to make a vow, do not rush and promise God it, and if you vow, write it down with you so that you do not forget it and may be faithful to God.

This verse and the one that follows are educational teaching about the vineyard and meeting the need of the hungry. The Law permits the passerby to enter another's vineyard to satisfy his hunger, and he may eat enough to satisfy his hunger, but he must not be greedy and carry some away with him as he leaves, taking advantage of the generosity of its owner.
Sickle: a curved iron tool with a wooden handle with which the farmer cuts the stalks of wheat after it ripens.

The same applies if a person enters a field owned by another, he may pluck the ears with his hands to eat as much as he needs, but he does not use a sickle to reap with, for the harvest is the right of the owner of the field, and he awaits its time to rejoice in it. The disciples of Christ did this when they were hungry and ate from the ears of the field (Mt 12:1-8).

Do not look with an eye of envy or jealousy at the possessions of others and covet them, especially if he treats you well, but be content with what you have and thank God, and if someone gives you something, thank him, so as to return love for love. And in proportion to your awareness of God's gifts to you, you will become contented, satisfied, and kind to everyone.
Divorce, marriage, justice, and compassion for the needy

If a man discovers a defect in the woman he has taken as a wife, a physical defect or one of conduct, which he sees as an obstacle to continuing a happy life with her, the divorce must not be verbal, but he must write a bill of divorce, give it to her, and send her out of his house.
Although God does not love divorce, He allowed it for the following reasons:
1- The man who hates his wife humiliates her and is harsh to her, so divorce is a liberation for her from this harshness, which the man at that time could have inflicted on her.
2- Writing a bill of divorce, which is done in the presence of accredited witnesses, gives the man an opportunity to reconsider if he was hasty in his decision.
3- The man who divorced his wife is not permitted to take her back if she has married another (v. 4), so that the man would not rush into hating his wife or divorcing her.
This law protects against the evil customs that the Egyptians had anciently, which was the exchange of wives if the men felt hatred for their wives.

If the divorced woman married another man and then the latter divorced her and gave her a bill of divorce, or died, she may not return to her first husband. This is considered an abomination, because the first husband considers his wife to have been defiled by living with another man, so he hates her more than before, and even if he shows willingness for her to return, he goes back to treating her badly. Therefore God forbade this kind of marriage, since it is considered a sin that defiles the Promised Land, which God purified by driving the pagans out of it so that His people might dwell in it.
Charged with any business ("a charge laid upon him"): any work for the benefit of the people is required of him.
This commandment shows God's concern for marriage, for it exempts one who marries for a year from taking part in the war and from all the works required for the community, for the following reasons:
1- So that he may have an opportunity for marital understanding and for adapting with his bride to the new life and forming good habits by which the two will live throughout their lives.
2- He has an opportunity to express his love and make his wife happy during this year, so that their good relationship is established and they rejoice all their lives.
3- So that the man will not be anxious about his bride during the war and so fail to attend to the responsibilities of war.
4- The man may be exposed to death in the war, and this would be very hard for his bride, who did not enjoy her marriage even for a year.

God's purpose in your marriage and in your being among people is that you form relationships with them that make them glad and make their lives happy. So try to express your love for those around you with words, smiles, gifts, or gentle touches by which you make them feel your love, and so you will strengthen your family relationships and gladden their hearts.
The mill: a tool for grinding grain consisting of two stones, an upper and a lower. The upper one moves and the lower one is fixed.
The upper millstone: the upper stone of the mill.

The Law forbids taking the whole mill, or one of its two stones, as a pledge for a debt. For the mill is the tool with which the grain from which bread is made is ground, so taking it means depriving its owner of his basic food and thus exposing his life to hunger and death.
Makes merchandise of him ("enslaves him"): from servitude, that is, makes him his slave.

If a Jew is found who is so hard-hearted that he steals one of his brothers to make him his slave or to sell him as a slave to others, this man must be put to death to remove the sin of harshness and theft, which in this case reaches the level of the sin of murder, because he has taken away a human being's life.

Do not hurt a person's feelings with wounding words, even if it is in reply to a wrong from him, for this is considered a moral killing, an insult, and the taking away of his rights as a human being accepted in society. Be tender, and you will enjoy the tenderness of God.

The Lord warns them of the necessity of applying the law of leprosy and of acting with all exactness on the instructions of the priests which the Lord taught them. (The details of the law of leprosy are given in Lev 13, 14.)

He reminds them of what happened to Miriam, the sister of Moses, when she and Aaron murmured against him after their departure from Egypt, that is, in the wilderness of Sinai, because he was alone in leadership, and God struck her with leprosy (Num 12) and they put her outside the camp in application of the law of leprosy. Miriam was not excepted because she was a prophetess or because she was the sister of Moses, and therefore the law of leprosy must be applied to all the people with all exactness.
Keep away from everything that defiles your thoughts and your senses, because you are a man of God, and so you will live pure and be able to feel God in your life, and He will bless you.

The purpose of this legislation is to preserve the dignity of the poor man if he borrows money from another person. It is not permitted for that other person to break into the poor man's house to take a pledge, because of the insult and humiliation this carries for the poor man; rather, the lender must stand outside the house so that the owner of the house may bring the pledged item out to him, and so that the creditor does not wrong the poor man and take from his house something more than the pledge. Justice must be applied however poor or weak the person is, because the creditor may become covetous when he sees the contents of the poor man's house and demand the pledge of many belongings in payment of his debt, or may go back on lending to him, demanding that he sell what he has and meet his needs.

If a person needs money and is compelled to pledge his garment, and if he cannot repay the money within that day, the creditor is bound to return his garment to him, because it is his essential need to cover his body while he sleeps.
Your gates: your cities.

The Lord commands that the hired servant who works for another for wages not be wronged, especially if he is poor, whether he is an Israelite or one of the strangers dwelling in the various cities of Israel.

Do not delay giving him his wages for which he worked, day by day, for he needs them and has exhausted himself the whole day to earn them. For if he feels wronged by the one he worked for, he will complain of him to the Lord, and the Lord will judge the wrongdoer and punish him for his injustice.

This law makes clear each person's responsibility for his own sin, so a judge is not to sentence a father to death because of his son's sin, nor a son because of his father's sin, as He affirmed in (Ezek 18:4). But the visiting of the iniquity of the fathers upon the children (Ex 20:5) means the spread of sin from the fathers to the children, who learn it from their fathers, so God repays the fathers and the children, each for his own sin. But if the children refuse to continue in the sin of their fathers, God will not punish them.

Be just in your judgments; do not be swayed by sweet words, and do not favor the rich and the strong, or a relative or a friend, but hold to the truth for the sake of God, who stands before you, and He will protect you from many injustices, and will be just with you, and will reward you for all your good works with eternal life.
The Lord demands justice in judgments, so the stranger is not to be wronged because he is not of the children of Israel, nor the orphan, because he has no one to defend him or claim his right.

Likewise, it is not right to take as a pledge the garment of a widow, which is her covering and her protection from cold and heat (as mentioned in v. 13); rather, lending to her is to please the Lord and a generosity on the part of the lender.

He reminds them of the bitterness of exile and need when they were enslaved in the land of Egypt and nothing delivered them from it except the intervention of the Lord who redeemed them. So as they experienced misery and suffering, they can appreciate the need of the wretched for mercy and compassion, and hasten to rescue them from their misery. He therefore commands them that, as He did with them and rescued them, they also should do the same with these.

In this verse and the following verses to the end of the chapter, the Lord teaches them the principles of works of mercy toward the poor. In this verse the Lord commands them that when they harvest their fields, if they forget a sheaf of the harvest in the field and remember it, they are not to go back to get it, but leave it for those who need it among the strangers, orphans, and widows who go out into the fields to gather what remains after the harvest for their necessary food. If they do this, the Lord will bless all their works and increase their good things, as He said in (Lev 19:9, 10, 2 Cor 9:6).

The method followed for harvesting olives was that the fruit of the olive branches was made to fall to the ground by means of long sticks. Here too the Lord commands them that the berries that may remain on the branches are not to be gone back for, but are also left for the same needy groups mentioned above.
You shall glean it ("go over the boughs again"): you pick up the leavings of the picking.
The same applies to the gathering of clusters of grapes from the vineyard. Do not go back again to pick what remains on the vine of the grapes, but leave it as a portion for the needy groups.

He encourages them in the previous works of mercy by recalling the feelings of humiliation and poverty that they suffered in the days of bondage in Egypt, so that they may hasten to have compassion on the needy.
Justice, penalties, and the brother's widow
God calls the judges to justice in acquitting the righteous and punishing the guilty when they are asked to judge in any quarrel or dispute.
He tells us about the punishment of the guilty by beating or flogging them, and he stipulates the following for it:
1- The flogging is to be done before the judge, so that he may be sure that it is carried out in the amount that he sentenced.
2- The stripes are not to exceed 40 stripes, lest the guilty man feel more humiliation and contempt than he can bear, and so that he does not faint physically or die.

It appears here that the purpose of the punishment is discipline and not humiliation. Christ was struck 39 stripes, and if we add the crown of thorns and the spear the number becomes 41; this is what the Church cries out in every prayer, saying "Lord, have mercy" 41 times, because Christ bore these sufferings on account of our sins.

If you are in charge and order discipline for a child or an adult, let it be within the limits of what benefits him and not what breaks him psychologically or physically. And may you convince him of the reason for the punishment, even if he is a child, and do not forget to show him also your love and your mercy.

It was the custom among the pagan peoples to put a muzzle on the mouth of the ox when it pulled the threshing sledge to thresh the various grains. But God's mercy appears in that He commands His people to let the ox eat the straw it needs so that it can continue its work. The meaning of this is kindness to animals, and all the more to man, so everyone who toils in a work should be rewarded, especially if it is the service of God, as is made clear in (1 Cor 9:9).

Take care to reward everyone who toils in any work, whether done for you or in the service of God, even if only with encouraging words, concern, and care, and if he is in need, attend to his material needs.

entries.section: (3) The law of marriage to the wife of the deceased

paragraphs.text: If a man dies and leaves his wife without having had a child by her, his brother is bound to marry her to raise up offspring, whose firstborn is counted as belonging to his dead brother. The brothers often lived together in one large dwelling, each with his family, as still happens in some villages. The new husband is responsible for his brother's widow, who has become his new wife, and takes care of all her needs, and it is not right for the wife to marry anyone other than her husband's brother unless this brother refuses.

entries.section: (3) The law of marriage to the wife of the deceased

paragraphs.text: If the husband's brother refuses to marry his brother's widow, as happened with the sons of Judah (Gen 38:8), and this shows that this custom was ancient, before the Law of Moses, the Law stipulates, to establish this heinous fault against the refusing brother, who fails to bear the responsibility and to preserve his brother's right to the inheritance of the Promised Land, which symbolizes the Kingdom of Heaven, that the widow of the dead man go to the elders of the city, who gather in the square at the gate of the city, and declare to them that her husband's brother refuses to bear the responsibility and to raise up offspring for his brother.

entries.section: (3) The law of marriage to the wife of the deceased

paragraphs.text: The elders try to persuade this brother to bear his responsibility and marry his brother's widow, and if he persists in refusing, the elders establish this against him by his plain confession; then, in contempt of this heinous conduct, the widow takes off this man's sandal and gives it to the elders as a testimony to his refusal to bear responsibility and a declaration that it is not permitted for him to walk on his brother's land, that is, his inheritance; and the widow spits in his face as a declaration of the contempt of the whole people for him, and they call his name all his life "The house of him that hath his shoe loosed," that is, the house of the one who refuses to bear his responsibility and who violates the Law.

After the brother's refusal to marry his brother's widow, they look for the nearest relative of the dead man, who is called the kinsman, as happened with Boaz and Ruth (Ruth 4), and if all refuse, the Law permits the wife to marry whom she wishes. Therefore in the Church of the New Testament the priest and the deacons take off their shoes on entering the sanctuary as a declaration that they are not the ones responsible for the salvation of people, but Christ alone is the Savior and they are only His servants. So too does every person at Communion, as a declaration of his weakness and his need of Christ his Savior.

Do not be negligent in your responsibilities, for you are a steward over them before God, and He will hold you to account for them on the Day of Judgment; and if you feel your inability, ask for His help, and He will not forsake you, and you will rejoice in experiencing His work in you.

entries.section: (4) The woman and the quarrel of men

paragraphs.text: His secrets ("his nakedness"): his reproductive organs.

If two men get into a fight because of a dispute or quarrel between them, and the wife of one of them comes and intervenes in the fight in order to rescue or support her husband against the other man, and she commits a shameful act showing impudence and recklessness, and even a desire to kill him, in that she seizes his private parts to force him to let go of her husband, the commandment here orders that this wife's hand be cut off, because by this she has cast off modesty and dignity and lost shame. Leaving her without punishment could cause others to stumble and encourage other women to do that act; therefore she is not to be treated with pity, but is to be an example to the others.
Do not be harsh in your dealings with people even if one of them provokes you and is insolent toward you, for self-defense does not mean revenge and an attempt to destroy the other.

God forbids cheating in weights and measures. The merchants used to carry the various weights in a bag in which they moved about, while the measures they kept in their houses. So it is not right for the merchant to have two weights, buying with the large and selling with the small, and likewise in measures (Lev 19:35, 36, Prov 11:1).

The Lord commands that one weight or measure be used for selling and buying, which is just and true, without cheating, for cheating in weights and measures is lying and stealing. If a person is honest in his dealings, the Lord makes his life on earth happy and blessed and gives him offspring who live always on the holy land. But cheating is an abomination to the Lord, and the curse falls on the one who commits it as a recompense for his deceit toward others.

Be honest in your dealings with others even if you have an opportunity to deceive them, and do not justify cheating by saying that you are in need and they are rich, or that they are thieves and so it is permissible to steal from them.
Amalek: a people descended from Esau, the brother of Jacob.
The Lord reminds them of the hostility that Amalek showed when they met the children of Israel on their departure from Egypt on their way to the Promised Land.

Amalek attacked the elders and the children who were weary from journeying from place to place in Sinai, who were slow in walking and lagged behind the group, and Amalek took advantage of their being separated from the rest, taking some of them captive and killing others. This act of theirs was evidence of their wickedness and of the absence of the fear of God in their hearts. Had they been honorable warriors, they would have come forward to confront and fought the strong of the people, and not the sick and the weak (Ex 17:8).

The Lord commands them here that, when they are settled in the land He gives them and have rest from the labors of travel and the wars with their enemies around them, they are to destroy the Amalekites and remove any trace of them from the face of the earth, so that they may never rise again.

The Lord warns them against forgetting to carry out this command, because the continued existence of Amalek constitutes a permanent danger to their peace, and this was done in many stages, as in (Num 14:45, Judg 3:12-20, Judg 6:3, 33, 1 Sam 27:8, Job 4:14, Isa 3:1-9) until they perished completely, so that they no longer exist now.

Injustice is always temporary, and the time will come when the injustice falls as punishment on the head of the wrongdoer. So do not persist in taking away the rights of others by not giving them an opportunity to defend themselves, or ridiculing their words, or using your authority in any way to restrict their freedom.
The firstfruits and the tithes
The Lord completes the commandments that the people are to begin to apply when they enter and settle in the land He gives them.

The one presenting the firstfruits must put them in a basket and carry them to the place where the house of the Lord is. The firstfruits were presented at the Feast of Pentecost (Ex 23:16, Lev 27:26), and if that was not possible, they were presented at any time.

When the one presenting the firstfruits reaches the place, he hands the basket to the priest serving in those days and makes a verbal confession before the priest that he has indeed entered and possessed the land that the Lord promised the fathers of the people to give them. By this, every presenter of firstfruits from the people of Israel acknowledges that the Lord God is the one to whom credit is due for their possession of the land and its good things, from which these firstfruits come.
The priest takes the basket from the one presenting it and places it before the altar of burnt offering, and this means presenting it to the Lord.
A Syrian ("Aramean"): of the people of Aram, who lived in the north of Iraq.

Wandering ("ready to perish"): Jacob, the father of the fathers, wandered in the lands of Aram, just as Abraham had first migrated from there. The person offers a prayer of confession extending to (v. 10), in which he summarizes the Lord's dealings with His people from the time of the fathers Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, for they belonged to the Aramean people. Then Jacob went down to Egypt to meet his son Joseph and sojourned there, and his family who accompanied him to Egypt numbered no more than 75 persons, including Jacob and Joseph and his sons. But during their stay in Egypt their number increased greatly, as did what they owned of cattle and sheep and of wealth in general.

Pharaoh took notice of the growing importance of the people of the children of Israel and feared the increase of their strength, so he stirred up persecution against them and subjected them to bitter slavery, exploiting them in works of building and farming.
The people cried out, complaining of their condition to the Lord, and the Lord heard their groaning, knowing the harshness of treatment to which they were exposed, which wearied and humiliated them.

God brought them out with power after He struck Egypt with the ten plagues, and led them by the pillar of cloud and the pillar of fire. Then He split the Red Sea and they crossed over to the wilderness of Sinai, and He drowned Pharaoh and his army in the Red Sea, and so saved His people from destruction.
The Lord led them on a long journey to the place where they would settle, which is the Promised Land, promised to their fathers, and it is one of the best of lands, abounding in much good.

And now, O Lord God, behold, I have brought the firstfruits of the produce of the land which You gave us, in acknowledgment of what You have done with us and Your great love toward Your people, for You are the owner of all these good things. Then he takes the firstfruits in his hands and sets them before the altar and bows down in thanksgiving and glorification.

This person enjoys the rest of the good things after presenting the firstfruits, taking care to feed the Levites, the poor, and the strangers from these good things, so that all may feel that they are one family eating from God's hand.
Thank God every day for His gifts, and take care to give some of them to the needy, because you are all members in the Body of Christ, which is the Church.

The tithes were carried to the place of the temple for two successive years, but in the third year, which was called the year of tithing, they paid the tithes in their cities and gave them to the Levites, the strangers, the orphans, and the widows to eat and be satisfied, so that it would be an opportunity for the sick and the poor who were unable to travel to the Lord's temple in Jerusalem to eat from the feasts made from the tithes for the needy and rejoice in God's gifts.

And they were to recite the confession mentioned, which extends to (v. 15), after paying the tithes. In it the one confessing declares that he has taken out what is holy (and the word "holy" means set apart) for the Lord, meaning the tithes, and has given it to the Levites, the strangers, the orphans, and the widows as the divine Law requires, and has not departed from it or ignored it.

The one presenting the tithe, or any of God's gifts, affirms at the end of the previous verse and then again at the end of this verse that he listens to the voice of the Lord and acts according to what He commands him and does not turn aside from it to the customs and practices of the pagan peoples around him, and he eats of the feasts made from the tithes for the Levites, the poor, the strangers, and all the needy (ch. 14:22-29) as a fellowship of love with these groups, so that all may feel unity and there be no feeling of superiority on the part of the giver who presents the tithe over those who receive. The following is observed in these feasts.

"I have not eaten of it in my mourning," that is, he has not eaten of the holy food which those who share in mourning for the dead are not permitted to eat. Likewise it was among the customs of the pagan peoples to present to the god of fertility from the produce of the fields, and they mourned in remembrance of his death and gathered to eat of the produce presented to him on this occasion of remembrance; he does not take part in these pagan customs.

"Nor have I taken away ought thereof for any unclean use," the law of purity that bound the children of Israel to observe it when eating of the holy things did not exist among the pagan peoples, who set no value on bodily purity. But he, as a devout Jew, keeps purity when eating of the holy things. Uncleanness means being defiled by burying a dead person or by uncleanness for any other reason.

"Nor given ought thereof for the dead," that is, he has not spent from the money holy to God on buying shrouds or any necessities for burying the dead, and likewise he has not offered from it to the false pagan gods, who are considered dead, that is, he has not offered from it to idols.
A prayer to the Lord after presenting the confession, asking Him to look down from heaven and bless His people and bless the land that He gave him and that He promised to the fathers.

Be careful, when you eat and drink and enjoy the good things of God, that your heart be pure from all evil, so do not judge anyone or hate him, and offer repentance for your wicked thoughts and every uncleanness, and you will rejoice in God's gifts.
Moses stresses to the people the importance of obeying all the commandments they have heard, and that this obedience be not only in outward performance but with all feeling and love.

You have already made a decision to follow the Lord and to walk in His commandments, statutes, and judgments, and to listen to all His teachings and submit to His commands, and not to walk in misleading ways like the other peoples.
And the Lord has promised you that you will be a holy nation to Him, which He attributes to Himself, and that He will be its leader and protector, as He promised your fathers before.

The Lord makes you a distinguished people, exalted in rank above all peoples, who acknowledge your good conduct and good reputation, so that you will be the object of praise of all the nations and have an exalted name linked to the name of the Lord, as it is said of you, "the people of God." And the peoples will marvel at the honor that has come to you, and you will become a people consecrated to the service of the Lord and the object of His love and care.

Obedience is your way to enjoy all of God's blessings, even if the commandments seem hard, but trust that they are the most fitting thing for your life, and you will receive blessings on earth because of them and glories in heaven that cannot be expressed. Writing the Law, with the blessings and the curses

entries.section: (1) Writing the Law and building the altar

paragraphs.text: Moses and the elders of Israel commanded the people to keep the divine commandments that the Lord gives them.

entries.section: (1) Writing the Law and building the altar

paragraphs.text: You shall plaster them with plaster: build them and coat them with lime.
Moses commanded the people that after they cross the Jordan River into the land the Lord is giving them, they should take large stones, set them up, and cover them with lime.

entries.section: (1) Writing the Law and building the altar

paragraphs.text: And they are to write on these stones all the words of the Law when they cross the Jordan, so that the Lord may help them to possess the land that He is giving them, which flows with many good things.

entries.section: (1) Writing the Law and building the altar

paragraphs.text: You shall whitewash them with lime: cover them with plaster.
Mount Ebal: today called Imad ad-Din, it lies north of the valley in which is the city of Nablus, which was anciently Shechem.

The Lord affirms a second time that after they cross the Jordan River they are to set up these stones and that they be set up on Mount Ebal and plastered with lime, and both Mount Ebal and Mount Gerizim, which will be mentioned later, enjoy a position in the middle of the holy lands, so that they are at the least possible distance from the edges of the land of Israel, so that all the tribes may make pilgrimage to them.

entries.section: (1) Writing the Law and building the altar

paragraphs.text: In addition to the stones on which you write the Law, you must build an altar to the Lord, also of stones, without dressing those stones with a chisel or an axe, but they are to be set as they are, and Joshua carried this out (Josh 8:30, 31). The altar here points to Christ, who is symbolized by Daniel in his vision (Dan 2:34) by the stone cut out without hands, for Christ was born without the seed of man.

entries.section: (1) Writing the Law and building the altar

paragraphs.text: He affirms again that the stones with which the altar is built are to be in their natural form, without any attempt to dress them with any tool.

entries.section: (1) Writing the Law and building the altar

paragraphs.text: And the offerings of thanksgiving to the Lord are presented, which are the peace offerings, which also signify rejoicing in the Lord and the offerer's gratitude for His great work done for him. It is the sacrifice of which a part is given to the priests to eat, which is the Lord's portion, and a part is eaten by the one offering the sacrifice, as a sign of the fellowship that believers live with God, and this is a type of the sacrament of Communion.

entries.section: (1) Writing the Law and building the altar

paragraphs.text: As the elders joined Moses in conveying the Lord's directions to the people, the priests join him here in leading the people and helping them to live in fellowship with the Lord. They make the people understand that, now that they have become a people chosen by the Lord and set apart for His worship and for bearing His care, they must listen to the voice of the Lord their God and obey His commandments that He commands them now.

It is noted in the preceding ten verses that God cares for His people after their entering the Promised Land, that they may abide in His word and worship and not be influenced by the laws of pagan worship nor take part in them out of courtesy to the nations around them; therefore He asked two things of them:
1- Writing the Law on a wall or on pillars of stone, so that when they pass by it they read it and remember the word of God and hold fast to His laws.

2- Setting up an altar of stones so that they remember that their worship is offered to God alone, whose Law is written beside this altar, and that they not offer sacrifices to any other god; for this altar is not for offering sacrifices upon it but a constant reminder of the worship of God, while the sacrifices are offered on the bronze altar in the tabernacle of meeting. With these verses the third sermon of Moses, which began from chapter twelve, ends. After that begins the concluding part, which includes the blessings and the curses, the song of Moses, the handing over of leadership to Joshua and the Levites, the writing of the Law, and then the death of Moses.

Read the Bible every day so that you learn the word of God, meditate on it, and apply it in your life, and remain a child of God, so that you are not influenced by the thoughts of the world around you, and your heart worships Him in the Church and is not occupied with the gods of the world, which are money and position......
Moses commanded the people to arrange their ranks and stand in a particular order after crossing the Jordan River, in order to recite the blessings and the curses.

Mount Gerizim: it is opposite Mount Ebal, which was mentioned in (v. 4), and is called today Mount at-Tur, and lies south of the valley in which is the city of Nablus (Map 18). He divides the tribes into two parts: six tribes on one side stand on Mount Gerizim, and they are the tribes of Simeon, Levi, Judah, Issachar, Joseph, which includes the two tribes of Ephraim and Manasseh, and Benjamin. This signifies that some of the people obtain the blessings, and they are those who obey the commandments of God and His Law; it is not meant that these tribes alone receive the blessings, but those from all the tribes who obey the word of God.

And the other six tribes stand on Mount Ebal as a symbolic indication of those upon whom the curses fall, and they are the tribes of Reuben, Zebulun, Gad, Asher, Dan, and Naphtali. What is meant here by pronouncing the blessings and the curses is the people's declaration that whoever does righteousness, the blessing comes upon him, while whoever disobeys and walks in evil, the curse comes upon him.
From here came the symbolic significance of dividing the people into two groups, for there will always be those who do good, as there will also be those who do evil.

The Levites: the priests are meant, who are from the tribe of Levi, as is clear from (Josh 8:33-35). The tribes stood at the two mountains, and those who pronounced the curses and the blessings were the priests standing in the middle of the valley, for they are the ones who light the way before the people and alert them to what is righteousness deserving the blessing and what is evil deserving the curse.

From this verse to the end of the chapter there are 12 warning commands beginning with the word "cursed," and there is no list of blessings because they are simply the opposite of the words of the curse. For whoever errs in one of the commands is cursed, and consequently whoever does not err is blessed.
Likewise the twelve laws mentioned are not the whole Law but a chosen group symbolizing all the Lord's commandments.

After each formula that the Levites pronounce, the people answer with the word Amen, which means "truly." The first curse: the subject of this curse relates to the second of the Ten Commandments (Ex 20:4, 5), for whoever carves an image or casts one to worship it as an idol does a work abhorred by the Lord, even if it is in secret, away from the eyes of people.

The second curse relates to the fifth of the Ten Commandments, which commands the honoring of parents (Ex 20:12), and the meaning of a person's making light of his parents is that he looks upon them with disdain and contempt and treats them lightly and does not honor them.

The third curse: the landmark is the boundary of ownership that separates the property of one person from the property of his neighbor, so it is a prohibition of coveting what belongs to others, as mentioned in (Ex 20:17), that is, in the tenth of the Ten Commandments.

The fourth curse applies in its literal meaning and its symbolic meaning. The literal meaning is that a person mocks a blind man and so leads him astray from the right way, or ridicules someone with some infirmity. The figurative meaning is intended for one who deceives the simple with misleading counsel or teaches the ignorant corrupt teaching.

The fifth curse: a commandment repeated many times in this book, concerning the weak in general and those who have no human support. The Lord forbids wronging them or infringing on their rights or departing from truth and justice in judging for them.

The sixth curse: this verse and the next three verses are a group that points to forbidden sexual practices and relate to the seventh commandment (Ex 20:14). The skirt: the edge of the garment; and since husband and wife are one, it belongs to the husband as it belongs to the wife, so his father's skirt means the skirt of the garment of his father's wife, that is, committing adultery with her. This deed is abhorred by the Lord, so it is never right for a person to have relations with his father's wife, whether in his father's lifetime or after his death, for the son must not violate his father's sanctity.

The seventh curse: this heinous deed was common among the pagan peoples. The Lord warns His people against everything that takes them away from holiness and brings them down to base levels and perverse sexual practices.
The eighth curse, which is one of the forbidden marriages (see Lev 18:9, 20:17), where this was considered a shame that required the cutting off of those who commit it from the sons of their people.

The ninth curse: marrying the mother-in-law or falling with her into sin was a contemptible and unclean act whose punishment was severe, burning with fire, because she is considered his mother (Lev 20:14).

The tenth curse: this curse recalls the sixth of the Ten Commandments, which forbids killing (Ex 20:13); for the crime of murder, even if it happens in secret without the murderer being known, the Lord who knows hidden things will punish the one who commits it. The neighbor here means any member of society.

The eleventh curse: whoever sheds the blood of an innocent person, whether by taking payment for it or by sentencing him to it judicially without right, by taking a bribe in return for the judge's issuing this sentence, the curse of God falls upon him.

The twelfth curse: whoever does not care about all that the books of the Law contain of commandments, judgments, and teachings, so as to hold fast to them and apply them in his life and act according to them, is cursed by God.

From here we understand the words of the Apostle Paul in (Gal 3:10), "For as many as are of the works of the law are under the curse: for it is written, Cursed is every one that continueth not in all things which are written in the book of the law to do them."

Only One obeyed all the Law and fulfilled all righteousness and accepted the curse for us, hanging on the cross, although He alone is good: the Lord Jesus Christ, who moved us from the bondage of the Law to the freedom of the glory of the children of God.

The commandment is a lamp and the Law is a light that illumines our way so that we know what is good for us. The more we listen to the word of God, the more we receive the blessing and escape the curse.
The details of the blessings and the curses
The Lord begins by specifying the condition for obtaining the blessings and avoiding the curses, which is obedience to the commandments of God, which raise His people above the other peoples.

In the previous chapter the Lord mentioned the transgressions that bring the curse on those who commit them, and consequently whoever avoids them receives the blessing. In this chapter the Lord gives detail about the nature and character of those curses and blessings, beginning with the blessings in (vv. 3-14). The following appears in this chapter:
1- God's justice and His punishment of everyone who persists in evil.
2- His mercy and His blessings to everyone who obeys Him.
3- The necessity of holding to His commandments in order to keep His grace, for His choosing of His people and His care for them do not prevent punishment from them if they reject His word.

4- His mercy in accepting the repentance of His people if they return to Him after the curses have come upon them, so that He lifts them from them and restores His blessings to them, as appears in (ch. 30).

This verse is an extension of the word "overtake" concerning the blessings, which came in the previous verse. The meaning is deep and wonderful: the blessings run to him to overtake him, instead of his running after them to overtake them. Wherever he is, whether in the city practicing an industrial or commercial trade, or in the village practicing agricultural work, the blessings will certainly come to him in all his works.
The blessing includes all the product of a person's works, and it is as follows:
1- The fruit of the womb, meaning offspring large in number and good in kind.
2- The fruit of the ground, meaning an abundant harvest.
3- The fruit of the livestock, of cattle and sheep, that is, what the animals bear is also large in number and in good health.

In the Divine Liturgy our Church prays the prayers of the Litanies (Awashi) according to the three seasons of the agricultural year: for the Lord to bless the waters of the rivers in the period from 12 Paoni to 9 Paopi; for the crops and the plants of the field in the period from 10 Paopi to 10 Tobi; for the fruits of the earth in the period from 11 Tobi to 11 Paoni. From this we see that the rites of our Church go back in their origins to the words of the Holy Bible, for in these prayers she hopes for God's blessings and His promises of good things.
