Moses, the man of God, that is, His servant who belongs to Him, blesses his people before leaving them, with words of comfort and encouragement that include prophecies and petitions for each tribe.

The Lord came from Sinai: the glory of God appeared on the mountain in Sinai before all the people, and He gave Moses the commandments and the Law (Ex 19, 20). This was in a cloud and lightnings and thunders and great fire and the sound of a trumpet.

He rose up from Seir unto them: the light of God was reflected from Mount Sinai onto Mount Seir, which is a chain of mountains inhabited by the descendants of Esau. This means that God gives light to Jews and Gentiles and wants the salvation of all, and this was accomplished in the New Testament.

He shined forth from Mount Paran: the glory of God was also reflected onto Mount Paran, which lies also south of Palestine and north of the wilderness of Sinai and is inhabited by Gentiles, that is, God wants the salvation of the Gentiles.

He came from the ten thousands of the holy ones: ten thousands, that is, tens of thousands. And the holy ones means the assembly of the angels from heaven. That is, God humbled Himself from His glory and appeared in tangible form on the earth on the mountain, and gave His commandments and His Law, and even more than this, He humbled Himself in the fullness of time and became incarnate of the Virgin.

At His right hand a fiery law for them: the right hand always signifies strength and blessing, but God is unlimited, so He has no right or left. His Law is symbolized by fire because it enlightens the life of whoever walks in it and burns everyone who insists on violating it, in the eternal torment.

In this verse Moses the prophet shows the greatness of God, who humbled Himself from His heavenly glory and appeared to His people on the mountain and gave them His Law, while He seeks the salvation of the Gentiles also.

When the people of God saw His glory and His love for them, they loved Him with all their hearts, which were sanctified to Him, that is, devoted for Him to reign over them, and they came to be in His hand, that is, in His care and providence. This is what happened in the wilderness of Sinai when they lived as a special people who believe in God apart from the rest of the peoples, and He cared for them with all His love. And when they saw this love, they bowed at His feet to learn from Him His commandments and His Law, as Moses and the seventy elders sat at the foot of the mountain of the Law (Ex 24:9-11), and as God glorified the people gathered before the mountain (Ex 19:18, 24:4).

When the people sat at the feet of God, they submitted to Him and declared their acceptance of the Law that Moses received from the mountain from the hand of God, and they felt that it was the greatest thing they had received, for it is the inheritance they hand down to their children throughout the generations so that they may enjoy life with God. It belongs to the descendants of Jacob, that is, those who believe in God. And Jacob, or the new Israel, is the Christian people everywhere.
Jeshurun: by Jeshurun is meant the people of God who are beloved to Him (ch. 32:15), and He reigns over them and leads them and shepherds them, with all their tribes and their heads.

Contemplate the beauty and greatness of God and join in praising Him with the Church through the book of the Midnight Praise, so that your heart is attached to Him and the passing delights of the world no longer dazzle you.

Reuben sinned by lying with his father Jacob's concubine and so lost the blessing of the birthright (Gen 21:22, Gen 48). Likewise from his tribe came Dathan and Abiram, who joined with Korah in murmuring against Aaron and his sons alone having the priesthood, and the earth swallowed them (Num 16). Therefore Moses wishes for the tribe of Reuben and prays for it that it may live and not die out because of these errors, and that it may have many men of its offspring to defend it.

The blessing of Judah: the blessing of Judah is an intercessory prayer asking for the Lord's help for him in time of distress and the answering of his prayers when needed. "And bring him unto his people" means the return of his warrior men safely to their people, that is, to their wives and children.

His hands be sufficient for him: an allusion to the tribe's entering into many wars in which the rest of the tribes did not support it, and even at times fought against it, so its victory was by reliance on the Lord. "Be thou an help to him from his enemies" means asking God's help against the enemies of Judah, as happened with King Hezekiah in his victory over the Assyrians (Isa 37:36-38). And Christ, who came from the tribe of Judah, conquered death and the powers of Satan and accomplished salvation alone, for "all forsook Him and went away, and He trod the winepress alone, and of the peoples there was none with Him" (Isa 63:30).
The blessing of Levi. Thummim: means perfections.
Urim: means lights.

These were two stones that were placed on the breast of the high priest and used to know the will of the Lord when making a decision, so that one of them would light up if God agreed to the request (Ex 28:3). Your righteous man: the high priest, who is from the tribe of Levi and who carries the Urim and Thummim on his breast.
Massah: means strife.
Meribah: means testing. The two words refer to one place where the event of the water coming out of the rock took place, when the people murmured against the Lord and quarreled with Moses and Aaron.

The tribe of Levi was distinguished by the priesthood coming forth from it, which led the people in worship and in hearing the voice of God by using the Urim and Thummim. And the priests bore the murmurings of the people, as happened at Massah and Meribah, in the persons of Moses and Aaron (Ex 17:1-7).

He mentions an important principle of the priestly tribe, which is that they sacrifice even family and human relationships if these hinder them from serving the Lord. This happened in several events that the Holy Bible mentions, which show their zeal for the Lord and their disapproval of the deeds of their brothers, among them:

When they killed many of the stubborn who worshiped the golden calf, when Moses commanded the Levites, saying: "Put every man his sword by his side... and slay every man his brother, and every man his companion, and every man his neighbour," and "the children of Levi did according to the word of Moses" (Ex 32:27, 28). When Phinehas was zealous at the sedition of Baal-peor and killed Zimri and the Midianite woman (Num 25). And the tribe of Levi took no inheritance in the land, because the Lord is their portion; He provides for them and takes care of their needs.

It is to be noted that no blessing is mentioned for the tribe of Simeon because of its joining with Levi in the killing of the tribe of Shechem, and Jacob declared that his soul did not rest in their council. Levi mended his way, so God blessed him and set him apart for His service. Some say that in the Septuagint, at the end of this verse, there is the phrase "Let the number of Simeon be many."

Moses mentions here the functions and duties of the priestly service. He entrusted to the Levites the teaching of the people in the ordinances of the Law and the statutes of the Law, and among the duties of their functions is offering incense to the Lord with the prayers of the people. The priests also offered the sacrifices and burnt offerings to the Lord according to what the Law prescribed.
Loins: plural of loin, which is the back and the two sides of the back in man, and they are a sign of strength in him, and to smite through the loins of a man is to break his strength.

Moses prays for the tribe of Levi that the Lord may give it more spiritual and bodily strength to help it perform its work, and accept from it the offerings of the people and the rest of its priestly services, and destroy the strength of its enemies, that is, the enemies of the priests and the servants who resist the word of God and obstruct His holy work.
In the stories of the Holy Bible there are many events in which rebels resisted the priesthood and its work, and how the Lord fought those who resisted, such as:
Korah, Dathan and Abiram (Num 16). King Saul, who killed eighty-five of the priests of the Lord at Nob (1 Kgs 21, 22). Ahab and his wife Jezebel (1 Kgs 18:4, 19:10).

The blessing of Benjamin. God looks upon the tribe of Benjamin with a special look of love, since it is the faithful tribe that continued to live in the midst of the tribe of Judah, holding fast to the worship of God in Jerusalem and to submission to the king from the descendants of David, that is, the tribe of Judah, and the kingdom of Judah was formed of the two while the rest of the tribes separated from them. The Temple was built on Mount Moriah, which lies in the land of the tribe of Benjamin (2 Chr 3:1). Therefore He calls it "the beloved of the Lord," for God by dwelling in the midst of the tribe, they dwell around Him in safety. The Lord keeps it, keeps dangers away from it, lifts it above the troubles and problems of life, and walks with it in safety.

How sweet and great are the promises that the Lord gives to those who love Him, for by their taking refuge in Him and being faithful to His covenants He embraces them, blesses their lives and gives them the peace that surpasses all understanding, which David expressed saying: "He that dwelleth in the secret place of the most High shall abide under the shadow of the Almighty" (Ps 91).
The blessing of Joseph

Moses asks the Lord to bless his land "for the precious things of heaven, for the dew," that is, the rains that water the crops so that they give an abundant harvest, and the dew moistens the grass and herbs on which the sheep feed. "And for the deep that coucheth beneath" means the waters of the rivers, springs and fountains that he asks for in abundance so that the land of Joseph may give many crops and cattle.

"And for the precious fruits brought forth by the sun," which are the agricultural crops whose growth depends on the warm rays of the sun, "and for the precious things put forth by the moon," which are the plants that grow in the shade. What is meant by the two expressions is that the Lord may bless his land so that it is filled with abundant good things and various crops that the different forces of nature work to make sprout and grow.
The hills: the mounds.

And for the chief things of the ancient mountains: the Lord also gives him of the finest and greatest of what grows in the mountainous lands existing from of old, of trees and plants, and of the precious things of the lasting hills, that is, what grows on the heights and hills that remain forever and are always fruitful.
The tribe of Manasseh, which came from Joseph, took a fertile land east of the Jordan, and likewise the tribe of Ephraim, which came from him, took a fertile land west of the Jordan (Josh 17).

And for the precious things of the earth and fulness thereof: by the precious things of the earth is meant what it contains and is filled with of precious metals and costly stones. "And the good will of him that dwelt in the bush": the Lord gives good things to those with whom He is pleased, and Moses described the Lord here as dwelling in the bush, an allusion to the Lord's appearing in the bush when He called him to service (Ex 3), in which He announced salvation for His people and the many good things that Moses the prophet now asks for the tribe of Joseph.
And Moses asked the Lord that His blessing come upon the head of Joseph, as a figure of its coming upon the whole person, and the crown is the top of the head or the brow.

And Joseph was called "the Nazirite of his brothers" because the word Nazirite means one set apart from a group so as to be distinguished by qualities, matters or tasks different from the group. And Joseph was indeed so in several respects:
1- His father singled him out with a special love above his love for his brothers, and he did not share in their evils (Gen 37:2).
2- His brothers separated him from themselves, for they treated him differently from how they treated one another, so they envied him and hated him.
3- God gave him a distinguished success, different from all those around him, in the house of Potiphar or in prison and then on the throne of Egypt, and also made him lord over his brothers.

The firstling of his bull is his glory: Joseph's wealth, represented by what was achieved for the tribe of Manasseh in the bulls and firstlings of bulls that it possesses, for its portion was in the land of Bashan with its abundant pastures, which is a very great wealth and a source of riches and pride for it.

His horns are the horns of the wild ox: the two horns are the tribes of Ephraim and Manasseh, which branched from Joseph, as it says at the end of the verse that they are "the ten thousands of Ephraim, and the thousands of Manasseh." He gave the ten thousands, that is, tens of thousands, to Ephraim because Jacob gave the blessing of the birthright to Ephraim though he was the younger, so his number was greater than Manasseh's. The wild ox: a wild animal of the bovine family of great strength, whose horns are doubly curved, and with these mighty horns, which are a figure of the tribes of Ephraim and Manasseh, he wrestles his enemies until they flee before him to the farthest place they can flee to.

It is to be noted that the abundant blessing that Joseph received and the coming forth of two tribes from him is evidence of his obtaining the birthright because of his godliness, in place of Reuben, who lost it because of his adultery with his father's wife (1 Chr 5:1). From the tribe of Ephraim came great men such as Joshua, and from Manasseh also great men such as Gideon (Judg 6) and Jair the Gileadite (Judg 10:3). The blessing of Zebulun and Issachar:

Moses the prophet mentions the blessing of these two tribes together because they dwelt next to each other in the land of Canaan, for the land of Zebulun lies north of Issachar (Josh 19:10-23). Rejoice, Zebulun, in thy going out: the tribe of Zebulun engaged much in trade, so its sons go out to trade with the other peoples and rejoice in the gains of their trade.

And, Issachar, in thy tents: as for the tribe of Issachar, it was settled in its tents, going out little, and it worked in farming and the tending of cattle, as Jacob also prophesied for it (Gen 49:14, 15). They shall call the people unto the mountain; there they shall offer sacrifices of righteousness: the mountain meant is Mount Moriah, on which the Temple of God was built in Jerusalem (2 Chr 3:1). And the peoples are the tribes of the children of Israel and also the Gentiles with whom the two tribes traded, and to whom they preached and whom they called to worship God and offer sacrifices in Jerusalem. For they shall suck of the abundance of the seas and of treasures hid in the sand: among the causes of the wealth of these two tribes also were fishing and trade by sea, for the sea was the source of their riches like a mother nursing and feeding them, because they dwelt beside the sea, which is the Mediterranean, and also the Sea of Galilee. And the two tribes also enjoyed the minerals buried in the depth of the earth, which were another source of their wealth. The blessing of Gad:

Blessed be he that enlargeth Gad: the land that was given to Gad, east of the Jordan, was wide and far-spreading, and the men of this tribe were famous as strong men, so his saying about them "he dwelleth as a lion" likens them to the lion crouching to seize its prey.

And teareth the arm with the crown of the head: in his victories over his enemies he used to destroy them all, individuals and commanders. By the arm are meant the ordinary soldiers, and by the crown of the head are meant the commanders of the armies. And he provided the first part for himself: that is, his portion of the land was determined before the other tribes, for they took possession east of the Jordan before their brothers crossed to the west, and their land was fertile and among the best lands.

For there, in a portion of the lawgiver, was he reserved: the lawgiver is the legislator, that is, Moses the prophet, who allowed them to possess the land and leave in it their wives, children and cattle on condition that they cross over with their brothers the rest of the tribes and fight with them until they obtain their portions in the land, and then return to their possession. Reserved: the tribe of Gad dwelt between Reuben on the south and half the tribe of Manasseh on the north, so it was secure. And he came with the heads of the people: he crossed the Jordan at the head of the warriors to take part in the war with their brothers as Moses commanded them (ch. 3:18-20). He executed the justice of the Lord, and his judgments with Israel: that is, he carries out the judgment of the Lord on the pagan Canaanite peoples and His will in giving Israel possession of the lands of those peoples according to His promises to the fathers.

The tribe of Dan possessed in the south of Palestine a portion between the tribes of Ephraim and Judah and between the tribe of Benjamin and the Mediterranean Sea, so the place was cramped for them, therefore they wanted to seize another place. So they fought Laish, which lies in the north of Palestine, and lay in ambush for it in the mountains of Bashan, and attacked it and took it (Josh 19:40-48, Judg 18:27-29). They were brave like a lion's whelp, and from them came the mighty Samson (Judg 14, 15). The blessing of Naphtali

The portion of the tribe of Naphtali was west and south of the Sea of Tiberias, so he prays for it that it may rejoice in its good and joyful portion, whose source is contentment with what it owns and the favor of the Lord, who blesses its land with its fertile, rich soil. And it is enough blessing for those lands what was said of them and of the land of Zebulun in the prophecy of Isaiah, in the honor with which the Lord of glory honored them when light dawned upon them, the light of Christ, who served their cities in Galilee, as it is also recorded in (Mt 4:14-16).

The blessing of Asher. The portion of land that fell to Asher was an extremely blessed portion, for he dwelt in lands rich in olive trees and vineyards and succeeded in farming and trade, and his brothers, that is, the other tribes, loved him and he gained their favor for the good things they obtain from him.
Let him dip his foot in oil: a figure of the abundance of good, for the oil is extracted there from the olives whose trees grow abundantly in those lands.

Your bolts shall be iron and bronze: the bolt is what secures the closing of the door (the bar), and the meaning intended is that the lands of the tribe of Asher will be fortified and it will be hard for the enemy to break into them.
As your days, so your rest: it means that however long your life lasts, rest and peace are available to you, and there is no one or nothing that troubles you.

God wants to bless your life with blessings that surpass your mind... Open the way for Him by strengthening your relationship with Him, and when He gives to you, thank Him, and would that you asked for spiritual blessings before material ones, for they are what lasts with you forever, and their sum is that you love Him and cling to Him.

entries.section: (3) Thanksgiving to God for His gifts

paragraphs.text: Moses addresses "Jeshurun," that is, the beloved people, saying: there is no one like God and none equal to Him among the gods of the world or the creatures. He rides through the heavens upon the clouds to hasten and come down to the aid of His people. These are expressions in our human language that show the Lord's readiness to help and rescue those who love Him quickly. The Lord often appeared in the cloud on Mount Sinai, and in the event of the Transfiguration in the New Testament, and in His ascension to heaven, and in His Second Coming.
And his saying "in his excellency" means that the Lord's condescension to be in the midst of His servants does not diminish His power and majesty.

entries.section: (3) Thanksgiving to God for His gifts

paragraphs.text: The eternal God is a refuge to which His people flee, for it is He who protects them and shadows them. He upholds His people with His arms, and drives out His enemies before him and commands His people to destroy the enemies with His help.

entries.section: (3) Thanksgiving to God for His gifts

paragraphs.text: The fountain of Jacob: the springs of water in the Promised Land, which the descendants of Jacob enjoy and which water their fields.

When the people are assured of the protection of their God, they dwell in safety, enjoying the sight of the good land that overflows with good things, such as the wheat from which bread is made and the vines from whose juice they drink; and they enjoy likewise the falling of dew and rain from heaven, which preserves the fertility of the land.

entries.section: (3) Thanksgiving to God for His gifts

paragraphs.text: The prophet congratulates his people on their happiness and good, for the Lord distinguished them from all the peoples around them and chose them as a people for Himself, so they have no equal among the nations, and it is the people to whom the Lord gave victory not by human strength but He fought for them. The Lord is the one who protects His children, like the shield that the soldier uses to protect himself from arrows and blows, and He is also the power that defeats the enemies like the sword in the soldier's hand, so that they have dominion over their enemies and tread upon their high places, that is, their great leaders and their fortresses and walls.

Would that you contemplated God's great works with you and how, by His power, you overcame many wars of the demons, so that you are strengthened and not disturbed by your falls or any weakness in you, but rise and strive, confident of God's support for you.
The death of Moses
The plains of Moab: the eastern plain of the Jordan valley, immediately north of the Dead Sea.

Moses went up to Mount Nebo, which is one of the chain of the mountains of Abarim, and the top of Pisgah is its highest peak (Map 6, 8), which lies on the eastern bank of the Jordan opposite Jericho, which lies to its west. From there the Lord showed him the land that He would give to His people, in its various parts, and the first part mentioned was from Gilead to Dan. Gilead extends from east of the Jordan to the border of the Arabian desert, while Dan is the region that was called Laish and was then invaded by the tribe of Dan, which settled in it, and it is at the farthest north of the country (ch. 33:22, Judg 18).
The second part lies west of the Jordan and includes:
The lands of Naphtali: opposite the region that Dan seized in the north.
The land of Ephraim: it is west of the Jordan, opposite the land of Gad on its east.
And Manasseh: the part that lies west of the Jordan, in continuation of the portion of the half-tribe east of the Jordan.
All the land of Judah unto the utmost sea: central and southern Palestine, from the Dead Sea to the Mediterranean Sea.
The third part includes:
The south: southern Palestine, the Negev.

The plain: as the inspired text explains it, it includes the area of Jericho, the city of palm trees, that is, the region of Jericho lying west of the Jordan, whose site is now Tell es-Sultan. It was called the city of palm trees because palm trees abound in it. Unto Zoar: on the southeastern shore of the Dead Sea.

By Moses' seeing the land that He swore to the fathers Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, the Lord wanted to reassure him about the fate of his people, who would possess those lands, but He would not allow him to cross into it because he did not glorify the Lord with fitting glorification in the incident of striking the rock twice (Num 20:10-12).

As Moses looked toward the Promised Land, would that you lifted your eyes toward heaven and contemplated the beauty of the eternity God has prepared for you, so that your spiritual feelings are stirred and you become zealous for life with Him and for drawing souls to prepare with you for the Kingdom.

entries.section: (2) The death of Moses and Joshua taking up the leadership

paragraphs.text: In a valley: the plain.

Beth-peor: a temple of the god Peor, the god of the Moabites (Num 23:28) (Map 15). Moses died after he had looked upon the Promised Land and been comforted by God's promises that He gives to His children, and God took his body and buried it in the plain opposite Beth-peor. He hid his body lest the children of Israel find it and worship it because of their great love for him. His body remained hidden until the day this chapter was written, which was written by Moses' disciple Joshua the son of Nun, and his body is still hidden to this day. The devil tried to reveal the body of Moses, but the archangel Michael rebuked him and prevented him by the power of God from revealing the body, lest he lead the children of Israel astray (Jude 9).

entries.section: (2) The death of Moses and Joshua taking up the leadership

paragraphs.text: God gave Moses health until the end of his life, so he was full of vitality though his age had reached one hundred and twenty years, and likewise his eyesight remained strong so that he was able to see the Promised Land from afar.

entries.section: (2) The death of Moses and Joshua taking up the leadership

paragraphs.text: The period of mourning for Moses extended for a month of time, which is the longest period of mourning for great men. The Jews wept for him greatly because of their great love for him and his great standing among them. They had likewise wept for his brother Aaron for a month (Num 20:29), a period which signifies perfection.

entries.section: (2) The death of Moses and Joshua taking up the leadership

paragraphs.text: The Lord had previously asked Moses, near the end of his life, to lay his hand on Joshua to consecrate him for succeeding him in leading the people (Num 27:16-23), for God pours out upon him His holy gifts by the laying on of hands. And as the children of Israel listened to Moses, they listened to Joshua, because the Lord placed awe upon him, just as Moses commanded them to obey him.
Here appears the rite of the laying on of hands, which was confirmed in the New Testament (Acts 13:3) in the ordination of bishops and priests, and the Church practices it to this day.

entries.section: (2) The death of Moses and Joshua taking up the leadership

paragraphs.text: The service of Moses, extending forty years, and his works were not enjoyed by another after him, in addition to the patience, longsuffering and forbearance toward the stubborn people with which he was adorned. He alone had a special dealing with the Lord in speaking directly with Him (Num 12:6-8).

entries.section: (2) The death of Moses and Joshua taking up the leadership

paragraphs.text: God worked through Moses great miracles that He did not work with any prophet, which appeared in the ten plagues, the parting of the Red Sea, and God's care for His people in the wilderness for forty years, so that the Church calls him the chief of the prophets.

In proportion to your humility and submission to God, His work is manifested in you and He reveals Himself to you so that you enjoy His fellowship, and He defeats your enemies under your feet so that you live reassured and joyful.
A comparison between Moses the prophet and Christ. Moses was a type of the Lord of glory Jesus Christ in many respects, the most important of which are:

1- God chose Moses from the midst of his people to be a prophet and leader to them (Deut 18:15), and likewise Christ was chosen by Him from among His people to save them and redeem them (Jn 1:11, Mt 1:3, 16).

2- Moses was subjected in his infancy to a plot to destroy him by a wicked king, Pharaoh, and God rescued him from his hand by a great miracle, and many children died in this plot (Ex 2). Likewise King Herod tried to kill Christ in His infancy, but He fled to Egypt, and Herod killed many children in Bethlehem (Mt 2).

3- Moses lived a period of time in Egypt, the first forty years of his life, and then returned to it to bring his people out of it (Ex 2). And Christ fled to Egypt in His infancy and lived in it for a period of time and blessed it, and then returned to Judea (Mt 2).

4- Moses went down after forty years to visit his people to set them free by his strength, and then returned after another forty years to visit them and set them free by the power of God (Ex 4:29-31). And the Lord Jesus Christ became incarnate to visit His people, and He went about everywhere doing good (Lk 1:68-78).
5- Moses left the glory of the royal palace and went down to visit his people (Ex 3) to share their sufferings. And Christ came down from heaven incarnate to share our humanity (Phil 2:5-8).

6- When Moses tried to break up the quarrel between the two Jewish men, the wrongdoer resisted him. Likewise when Christ came to save His people, the priests and Pharisees rose up against Him and crucified Him.
7- Moses worked miracles to prove to his people and to Pharaoh that he was sent by God. And Christ performed many miracles to prove His divinity and that He is from heaven.

8- God spoke to His people through Moses, for He spoke to him and he told the people God's commands (Ex 19:7, 20:22). And in Christ the Word of God appeared to the whole world, so God spoke to His people through His life on earth (Jn 1:1, 14).

9- Moses fasted forty days to receive the commandments and the Law (Ex 24:18, 34:28), and Christ fasted forty days and was tempted by the devil (Mt 4) before beginning His ministry and giving humanity His life-giving words.
10- God gave His Law to Moses on the mountain (Ex 19, 20). Likewise Christ gave His Law in His Sermon on the Mount (Mt 5, 6, 7).
11- The face of Moses shone after he saw God (Ex 34:29, 30). And Christ's face shone in His Transfiguration on the mountain (Mt 17:1, 2, Mk 9:2-6).

12- The glory of God appeared before Moses in the cloud and the thick darkness on the mountain when he received the Law, and a cloud surrounded Christ on the Mount of Transfiguration, and at His ascension a cloud took Him out of the sight of His disciples.

13- God bore witness to Moses and glorified him before his brothers Aaron and Miriam (Num 12:8), and the Father bore witness to Christ at His baptism and in His Transfiguration by His saying "This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased" (Mt 3:17, 17:5) and His saying another time "I have both glorified it, and will glorify it again" (Jn 12:28).
14- Moses was followed by twelve tribes and seventy elders (Num 1, Ex 24:1, Num 11:16), and Christ had twelve disciples and seventy apostles (Mt 10:1, Lk 9:1, 10:1).

15- Moses appeared after his death in the Transfiguration on the mountain with Christ and Elijah (Mt 17:3), and Christ appeared after His death and resurrection to His disciples and to many (Mt 28:9, Mk 16, 1 Cor 15:5-8).

16- Moses declared his readiness to redeem his people by having his name blotted out of the book of life for the sake of the salvation of his people (Ex 32:32). And Christ actually redeemed His people on the Cross.
17- Moses died on a high place, Mount Nebo (Deut 34:1, 5), and Christ died on a high place, the Cross.
18- Moses resembled Christ in many qualities, such as:
a – Being mighty in words and deeds (Acts 7:22, Lk 2:47).
b - Gentleness (Num 12:3, Mt 12:20).
c - Meekness and humility (Num 12, Mt 11:29).
d – Forgiveness (Num 12:13, Lk 23:34).
19- Moses resembled Christ in many offices, such as:
a – Prophecy (Deut 18:15).
b - Kingship (Deut 33:4, 5, Mk 15:2).
c - Priesthood (Ps 99:6, Ps 110:4).
d – Mediation of the covenant (Ex 20:23, Isa 55:3-5).
e- Legislation: each of them gave the Law to his people.
f - Founding the Church: Moses established the tent of meeting, a type of the Church (Ex 40), and Christ founded the Church (Mt 16:18).
g - Judging and judgment (Ex 18:13, Jn 5:22).
h - Intercession): Ex 32:31, 32 – Jn 2:1-5.(
20- The life of Moses was accompanied by many phenomena that signify important matters in the New Testament with Christ, the most important of which are:
a – The bush: as a type of the Incarnation of Christ from the Virgin.
b - Crossing the Red Sea as a type of Baptism (1 Cor 10:2).
c - The manna: a type of the Body and Blood of the Lord (Jn 6:35, 50).
d – The rock from which the water comes out as a type of Christ (1 Cor 10).
e- The rod of Moses as a type of the Cross.
f - Circumcision as a type of Baptism.
g - The bronze serpent as a type of Christ (Jn 3:14).
h - The sacrifices, a type of the sacrifice of Christ on the Cross.
i - The feasts in the Old Testament as a type of the feasts in the New Testament.
j - The lifting up of Moses' hands in prayer in his war against Amalek (Ex 17) as a type of the Cross.
k - The tent of meeting, a type of the Church of the New Testament.
